utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is the 2nd of December, 2008. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Mundis, Ms. Biersay, and their associates, as well as Mr. Seselj and all the people assisting us in this courtroom. Before I give the parties the floor, the Trial Chamber will advise you of the following: I shall read it out slowly. This has to do with the comments made by the Registrar on the follow-up to the decision taken by the Trial Chamber relating to the privileged communication of the accused. Pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision relating to the privileged communication of the accused recorded confidentially on the 27th of November, 2008, the Registrar recorded publicly, on the 1st of December, 2008, comments in which he informs the Trial Chamber that pending the directives that will be given by the President of the Tribunal, who has been seized of this on the 1st of December, 2008: (A), has decided to authorise, on a temporary basis, privileged communication between the accused and Mr. Boris Aleksic, appointed as a member of the Defence team of the accused since the 24th of September, 2008, and: (B), contemplates to authorise, on a temporary basis, that the accused be entitled to receive faxes on a confidential basis from its Defence team in Belgrade. The Trial Chamber indicated to the Registrar that it hoped that this measure that it intends to implement be implemented as quickly as possible to enable the accused to prepare, as efficiently as possible, the cross-examination of the Prosecution witnesses. The Trial Chamber is satisfied with the follow-up to its decision of the 27th of November, 2008, provided by the Registrar, and hopes that the issue of privileged communication will be settled as soon as possible, whilst abiding by the rights of the Defence. This is what the Trial Chamber wished to state. Mr. Seselj, I know that you wanted to take the floor, so I shall give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's something new here, if you compare it to the letter that the Registrar sent me. It seems that they have made concessions to you and said that I could receive telefaxes in confidential form from my associates. Now, who I can receive them from, the Registrar doesn't say. How can I receive telefaxes until I send one out or before I give my associate instructions to talk to so-and-so and take a statement, and then in taking that statement, to steer him towards one subject or another? It's as if somebody is sending me telefaxes from the sky, dropping from the sky and statements from the sky. I absolutely do not accept this, and I do not accept that the Registrar of the International Tribunal has the right to interfere with my Defence. That is something I find quite unacceptable. And he cannot lay down conditions either. He says for my legal advisors, they gave public statements linked to the Tribunal in an inappropriate manner and acted in a way that could jeopardise the International Tribunal. Now, who is it who can say that somebody's statements were inappropriate; the Registrar? And then he says that the statements are inappropriate for which he's being criticised, in the moral sense and in other senses, too; next, to act in a way which can jeopardise the reputation of the International Tribunal. Now, only people can have my respect who consider that The Hague Tribunal has absolutely no good reputation at all, professional or moral. I can only believe those people. Anybody who thinks this Tribunal has a professional and moral reputation, I do not trust; and I'm not going to trust him with any assignment of mine. And I told you that at the very beginning of the trial, so you can't re-educate me in that respect, and that's the strategy of my Defence and indeed the style of my Defence; and I have every right to choose the type of Defence case that I wish to raise, first of all, by putting into question and challenging the legality of this Tribunal, and then all the rest of it. Furthermore, the Registrar refused to pay expenses for my associates, their travel expenses and others, and they will never come back again unless they are paid for their coming here more than two months ago. So I do not accept that the Registrar can choose from amongst my advisers and say, "This one is a good one, this one isn't." I am the sole person that can decide matters like that, and nobody will come in to see me until all three advisors plus a case manager can come in to see me altogether. Nobody is going to come in. I'm not going to receive any faxes. I'm not going to have any type of phone conversation. This man, this Aleksic, doesn't have an office at all, and now he has to be at home all the time waiting for me to call him up, if I'm to find him; whereas the Registry insisted, and you supported this Registry, that Slavko Jerkovic, as a professional lawyer, is the most appropriate and suitable; and that I can use his telephone and who knows what else, that finances go through him and all the rest of it. The Prosecutor will wind up his Prosecution case in a couple of months, and then the Defence case will start, but I can tell you that there will not be any Defence case. There won't be a Defence case until somebody brings the Registrar to task and say: "You're a clerk here and you have no right to meddle in matters of the Defence. You're here to deal with matters of discipline, hygiene, any other goods that need to be procured. You are there to pay out salaries and so on and so forth, but you cannot meddle in Defence matters." Now, if the Registrar is going to interfere, then there will be no Defence case. Somebody who is interfering all the time and tripping me up at every step, and I might fall at every step, being tripped up like that, so how long is that going to go on for, I wonder. No other obstacles are put in the path of any other trial, and I'm not going to accept them in this trial too, so you can consider that the problem has not been resolved and why you welcome this conduct on the part of the Registrar is your own affair, but I must say that I'm quite amazed at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, first of all the Registrar sent you a letter on the 28th of November, 2008. Therefore, you can respond to his letter and challenge what he states in his letter. Nevertheless, in this letter, the Registrar is asking you to give him the telephone number of Mr. Aleksic. As soon as you have done that, you will then be able to have your privileged communication with Mr. Aleksic. Let me remind you, and it is my colleague who indicated this to me, a moment ago you were the one who appointed Mr. Aleksic, so if you appointed him, you felt that he had at least a telephone number. You are saying that he doesn't have an office, but this is something which can be overcome. The Registrar is just asking you to give him the telephone number of Mr. Boris Aleksic so that you can communicate with him. This is a major step forward, as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned. This means that you can now contact someone whom you trust entirely. Now, as far as the faxes are concerned, of course in the letter that was sent to you by the Registrar, nothing is said about the way in which this will work out, materially speaking. There is a fax in this room, just outside the courtroom, and there is a fax at the UN Detention also, so I'm sure this problem can be overcome. I'm sure you can receive documents in this manner. The Trial Chamber feels that in light of all of this, this situation is definitely a step ahead and this is a step forward, compared with the previous situation. All we want is for you to be able to contact the person of your own choice. Nobody is interfering in your Defence. It's for you to appoint someone, and it's for you to handle, but it is important that the person you have appointed is someone whom you can contact. As you know, and you know better than anyone else, this was not an easy decision to take. Therefore, we have done our utmost and made sure that you are able to defend yourself as best as possible. On a personal note, I would like to say that as the Prosecution has 26 hours left to call its Prosecution witnesses, we hope that in that time that is left, we can focus on the substance in this case. We are spending a lot of time dealing with housekeeping matters and logistical matters, and we waste a lot of time over this. I had rather spend this time reading documents, the transcripts, to be able to, at the end of this trial, assess whether you are guilty or innocent. My time would be much better spent focusing on these matters, rather than having to write up decisions relating to problems that have arisen between you and the Registrar, between the President of the Tribunal and the Registrar. So let's wait and see. The Trial Chamber can only advise you to respond to the Registrar and to give Mr. Aleksic's telephone number as quickly as possible. I know that Mr. Mundis would like to take the floor, so I shall give him the floor, and then we shall bring the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, last Friday I said I had another question to deal with. I said I could wait for this week, if it's not too late. And it is about the previous witness under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there is another topic you would like to address. I apologise, Mr. Mundis. We shall deal with Mr. Seselj's second issue, and then I shall give the floor to Mr. Mundis. So what is this about, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I challenge the possibility of having double statements at all by witnesses appearing, and in particular the witness appearing last week, and that that could be taken under 92 ter. And I presented my arguments; first of all, because the main statement that was given was given to the Muslim authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Mostar, in fact, and the additional statement was given to The Hague Tribunal, the OTP. Now I'd like to draw your attention to some things that are in the statement themselves. You see in this main statement given to the Muslim authorities, it says that with the television crew from Novi Sad, six members of the White Eagles from Serbia arrived. And in the statement that was given to The Hague Tribunal, to the OTP, this is added on to in a paragraph, in the last sentence, when he says: "When I say 'White Eagles,' I meant Seselj's men." So there we have the Prosecution transforming the initial statement. And you have an example of that in another place as well, which is to be found on page 7 of the first statement. It says: "I said I didn't know about any of that, when an unknown soldier, a member of the White Eagles from Serbia came into the room and started beating me and the others accepted that." Now, in paragraph 28 of the additional statement taken by this Tribunal, it says the following in paragraph 26, I suppose: "I mention that an unknown soldier entered the room, a member of the White Eagles, I said. I think he was Seselj's White Eagle." So you just put that phrase in, "I think it was Seselj's White Eagle." So I just want to do illustrate this for you to see the methods The Hague Tribunal uses. Now, this witness under 92 ter, in his first statement, just tells us the story secondhand that he heard from ten young girls, members of the Seselj's army who were specialised in slaughtering civilians. So somebody told him about that somewhere. Now, the OTP, The Hague Tribunal, since that is not enough, and this is how witnesses are used, a typical example of how witnesses are used and how things are construed; so the first we had the arguments put forward last week that under no conditions can this be adopted under 92 ter and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you well, Mr. Seselj. If the Trial Chamber were to admit the statement presented by the Prosecution, as well as the statement presented by the Muslim authorities, then we could compare the two.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Perhaps you don't remember this from last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I objected and said that the statement was in two parts, you said, I assume, that just this part given to The Hague Tribunal should be admitted into evidence. And then the Prosecution put you right and said that they consider both statements to comprise a whole. That was the essence, that both these statements are treated by the OTP as one, as a whole. So if you have this supplementary statements given to the OTP, you cannot understand what it refers to unless you have the first statement that was given that was comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This procedure that the accused is now undertaking is completely improper. Every issue that he's raised with respect to these 92 ter statements were and could have been put to the witness during cross-examination of the witness. The accused has waived his cross-examination, and therefore it is inappropriate and improper for him to now be challenging the admissibility of those statements when he had the opportunity to cross-examine the witness, when he had the opportunity to question the witness as to any perceived discrepancies between the statements. He had that opportunity. He waived it. He's lost the chance to now argue with respect to issues that the witness very well might have been in a position to clarify. And so we would strenuously object to this type of procedure. It's not the first time it's happened, whereby the accused, having waived his cross-examination, subsequently attempts to make arguments on issues which could have been put to the witness, but which the accused opted not to do so by waiving cross-examination. It's improper, and we would strongly urge the Trial Chamber to put an end to this type of procedure. The Chamber has repeated inquired as to Mr. Seselj as to why he does not cross-examine 92 ter witnesses. He's indicated that he does that as a matter of principle. Of course, he must live by the consequences of his own decisions, including any decisions with respect to the waiver of cross-examination. These questions could have been put to the witnesses. He chose not to do so, and he must now suffer the consequences of the decision which he took and which forms part of his decision to represent himself in these proceedings and to pursue whatever type of defence he chooses to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your position is on the transcript. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The thing that Mr. Mundis is putting forward is completely nonsensical. I'm not interested in what the witness said and what it says in his statements. I am standing up here to oppose the illegal behaviour of the International Tribunal. That is the sole purpose of my taking the floor, and I'd like to tell you, as the Trial Chamber, that you cannot accept these two pieces of paper as a 92 ter statement. They're not in the form of a 92 ter statement or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj's position is on the record. Mr. Mundis's position is on the record. And the Trial Chamber will rule on this matter. We need to move on. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I again put on the record the Prosecution's objection, in the most strenuous terms, to the accused continuing to indicate that the Prosecution is undertaking illegal behaviour. That is simply not credible, it is simply ridiculous, and he continues to make a mockery of these proceedings and this Tribunal; and we object to that in the most vigorous terms. Your Honours, on the 25th of November, 2008, the Trial Chamber rendered a decision with respect to the Prosecution's motion to terminate the self-representation of the accused. The Prosecution would respectfully request that we be given an extension of time, until Friday of this week, that is, 5 December, in order to make a determination as to whether we will seek certification to appeal part or all of that decision, pursuant to Rule 73(B). A final decision has yet to be taken. The deadline otherwise would expire today at midnight, and we would ask for an extension of time until Friday, 5 December, in order to make a determination, and if so determined, to file a request for certification of that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know full well that as far as deadlines are concerned, the Trial Chamber is always very flexible. Therefore, you have until Friday at midnight to file potential or certification to appeal that decision. I shall now ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom, and Ms. Biersay will tell me how much time she will need for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As the Court is aware, this witness came to the Netherlands only this morning, and I was able to meet with him only this morning very quickly. I actually concluded meeting with him at approximately 1.00. And I think we can start with 90 minutes, but due to the abbreviated nature of my meeting with him, I would ask the Court to consider, if the need arises, to extend that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the witness only arrived this morning, because on Sunday there were problems at the airport in Sarajevo due to the snow. Therefore, the plane could not take off on Sunday. That is why this witness could only arrive this morning. Ms. Biersay only had a short time with him this morning. Good afternoon, Witness. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like us to clarify one point. I received information on the 28th of November, according to which there would be two possible ways in which this witness would be examined, as well as Sulejman Tihic. One variant is that if VS-029 comes in and the second option is when -- if the witness does not come in. Now, I still have not been informed whether Witness VS-029 is coming in to testify. I would have to know that today or not. If he is not coming in, then two hours have been allotted to Mr. Banjanovic and two hours for Mr. Tihic. That is my written information. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And is VS-029 coming in? That's my main question, actually. Or is that going to be a strategic surprise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, VS-029 is not coming. Is that right, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As far as we know, that is the case, Mr. President. He, at this stage, is refusing to travel. I will keep the Chamber and Mr. Seselj appraised of any changes in that situation. If he were to travel, it would most likely be today, in which case I will have sufficient information tomorrow to indicate whether or not he will appear. It, at this stage, does not appear likely that VS-29 will be testifying this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have the updated information on this issue. We don't know any more than you do. Witness, can you give us your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Fadil Banjanovic. I was born on the 4th of July, 1962, in Kozluk, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an MP in the Chamber of Nations in the Parliament of Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are a member of Parliament, elected. What is your political affiliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Social Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, into the Parliament of Republika Srpska then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. MP. Have you already testified in a court, and if so, could you tell me in what case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the case against Mr. Milosevic, in the case that had to do with the Zvornik group in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Milosevic trial, were you a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I spoke about deportation, about expulsions of Bosniaks, so that is to say that I was a Prosecution witness against Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in Belgrade, on whose behalf did you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, I was a Prosecution witness, testifying for the Office of the Prosecutor there about deportations of Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you've already testified, so you know how things are going to occur. You know that at first you will be asked questions by Ms. Biersay, questions that are going to be put to you by the Prosecution. You have met Ms. Biersay this morning, but only shortly, because of your flight problems, but you did meet her, however. And she will put some questions to you. After this phase, Mr. Seselj, the accused in these proceedings, will put questions to you, and this will be in the framework of his cross-examination. You will have to answer his questions. The three Judges in front of you on the Bench can also intervene at any moment to ask questions in relation to your answers. Try to be as specific as you can in your answers. But given your past activities and your present activities, I'm sure that you will be able to be very concise. If you do not understand the question, don't hesitate to ask for the question to be reformulated. We have 20-minute breaks every hour and a half. If your testimony is not finished tonight, you will have to come back tomorrow, tomorrow at 8.30, because we'll be sitting in the morning tomorrow. We are sitting this afternoon, but this is quite exceptional. We should have been sitting in the morning. So if you are done with your testimony by the late afternoon, you will have so come back tomorrow. But now you are a witness of justice. You are no longer in contact with the Prosecution. You can only answer their questions. I wanted to say all this so that these proceedings could be as smooth as possible. Ms. Biersay, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described for the Court that you are currently an MP with the Chamber of Nations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how long have you held that position?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is my fifth year now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For the period of 1984 to 1992, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Kozluk, the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What position did you hold in that village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was one of the top people in that very small town. I was president there. I held a few other posts, like president of the Hunting Association, and I was a person who enjoyed quite a reputation in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could now ask for 65 ter number 7425, please, which, for the Judges, would be the last one in your binder, which is arranged in 65 ter number order.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the bottom of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you place your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of May, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is 65 ter number 7425, is that a summary of your educational and professional background?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, we'd ask for the admission of 65 ter number 7425.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps the witness didn't notice that, but I don't think that this can be admitted into evidence before this is cleared up. In bullet point number 7. The statement was probably taken in English and then re-translated into Serbian, and the Serbian makes no sense whatsoever. It says here that Mr. Banjanovic was "nadjalnik [phoen]" of Kozluk until 1992. There was never such a post in Kozluk. He knows that better than I do. So it's the translation that's a problem. He probably said that he was president of the Local Commune, and that is what the wording was supposed to be, "pretsednik mesna" [indiscernible]. So I'm drawing your attention to that. I want to say yet again that it is nonsensical to take statements first in the English language and then to re-translate them into Serbian, and then they make no sense whatsoever in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it may be best to have the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would respectfully submit to the Court that this is appropriate cross-examination. The witness has said that he can identify the document, that he's reviewed the document and signed the document. If Mr. Seselj has other things he would like to bring up, it would be appropriate for him to use his time in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I was about to give a final number to this document, but we'll only give it an MFI, according to your wishes. So if we could please have an MFI number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P661, marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will rule in the end. Continue, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The document that you just saw on the screen, is that a document you had reviewed, in your own language, and signed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could now have Exhibit number P302, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber where Kozluk is relative to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Kozluk is a nice little town. It's on the road between Zvornik and Bijeljina, on the banks of the Drina River. It is surrounded by several settlements inhabited by a majority Serb population. But in other places, like Sepac and others, Bosniaks are the predominant population. Kozluk was a multiethnic community where Bosniaks lived, Roma, Serbs, and a few Croat families. Kozluk is a local commune within the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Approximately how far is Kozluk from the town of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: About 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you described Kozluk as being a nice little town. I'd like to direct your attention to the beginning of 1992. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, on the map, I don't see Kozluk at all on this map. Is it on the map? Yes, I see it. Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could perhaps enlarge that area. There are two areas that are highlighted in yellow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is much more legible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And looking at this map, does that reflect the areas that you just discussed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Kozluk, Tabanci, Malesic, Skocic, Trsic, Sepac and so on, nice places on the banks of Drina River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, there's a mystery here on this map. We see Kozluk with a big red dot, and on top of this "Kozluk" in bold, there's a smaller red dot with another "Kozluk." So are there two Kozluks? There's a Kozluk next to the river and another one that's further away from the river, so could you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's just one single Kozluk, there's just one Kozluk, and that's this biggish sign over here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, on top of the big red dot, there's a smaller red dot, and it's also written "Kozluk" above this small red dot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Biersay is showing us a map with a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been previously admitted as Exhibit P302, and I think it is helpful for the witness to explain that that is an error, the one that we see in shadow, that is, the small one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But the one in bold, is that where it should be for Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. MP, you know all this. You know this area very well, so could you tell us what is the real name of the town on the small dot, written "Kozluk" in grey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are several places here where there is a Serb population, so you see all these places where there is a Serb population, and Kozluk is just where the little red dot is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, the city of Kozluk is everything that is in yellow, that is the whole area of the city of Kozluk, and in this surface there's this red dot with "Kozluk" written on it, but there's only one town called "Kozluk."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber that period in time when you noticed things had begun to change in the nice little town of Kozluk? And specifically I'm referring to 1992.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a new things for all the citizens was the entry or passing through of a large number of trucks or vehicles, and there were young men in these vehicles and they were deployed in Tabanci, Malesic, Skocic, these surrounding Serb-populated places. For me, personally, and for many citizens of Serb ethnicity, these were people and vehicles unknown to us. At first, we didn't even know what this was all about. However, what people noticed in public was that more than more people like this were coming in. They called themselves military reconnaissance or scouts. And we talked to other ethnic Serbs who were our neighbours, and we concluded that these people were building roads, digging trenches. All of it looked like some kind of preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when there were barricades that were set up in the Kozluk area?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know who set those barricades up?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they introduced themselves as the Serb Territorial Defence, because the Serb municipality had already been established, also a Serb MUP, Serb Territorial Defence. And even in Kozluk or around Kozluk, barricades were built, made of wood, and there were armed guards there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you please describe for the Trial Chamber what these armed guards looked like?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had the opportunity to see that everyone and everything Serb was armed. Even mentally-handicapped people, like a man nicknamed "Curica," meaning "little girl." All these people were fully armed. There were quite a few persons whom I did not know, who had simply come from elsewhere. They had different uniforms, they had different insignia, and one could see among the local population that these military scouts, as they called themselves, were the bosses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did any of these people you just described tell you who had invited them, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in some conversations with some people who were military commanders, like this Pejic, Zuco, Pivarski, Niski, often we would sit and talk, and then I'd ask, "Why are you here?" And they said: "Well, the Serb authorities called us, President Grujic, the top people of the Serb municipality. They called us to protect our Serbian brethren from the Muslims who were armed and those murders would happen and so on." This commander Zuco said this to me several times, and this other commander Pejic, and also some local Serbs were saying that some units and some people would come in to help, people that were well armed, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You mentioned someone by the name of Grujic, and you call him "President Grujic." What is the full name of Grujic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Branko Grujic is a baker. His son went to school with me, so I know the family. Brano Grujic, when this Serb municipality was established, the Serb municipality of Zvornik, he was the first president of that Serb municipality. And in some conversations with some people, they said that they were the leadership of the Serb municipality and there it was Branko Grujic, who had called these people in to help clear up the situation in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Around the time that you observed these forces coming in, the ones that you've just described, was there anything being transmitted on the radio to the population of your village in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the area of Kozluk and this broader area did not have its own television or its own newspaper. There was just this radio station that could be heard from Loznica, Radio Loznica. And then there was Radio Zvornik, too. It was Radio Loznica in particular that called Bosniaks, Muslims, daily to surrender their arms, to surrender their cannons. There was this warmongering going on all the time, in terms of media propaganda, to sew discord among the people. They kept saying that we should hand in our cannons, and they were sending the police in, and these two radio stations played a highly negative role as far as Zvornik is concerned. We, as citizens, were forced to listen to these broadcasts because we didn't have any television, we didn't have any newspapers of our own, so this left a highly negative impression on ordinary citizens, this constant talk about war, about the hand-over of cannons, Zoljas and stuff that we had never heard of until then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The radio stations that you just mentioned, were they broadcasting only to Kozluk or to other places as well?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the broadcasts came from Loznica, a town in Serbia, and Zvornik in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but these radio waves could be heard up and down the Drina River. The radio frequencies were such that we could hear this well in Kozluk, but also beyond.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What concerns did you have, based on what you were seeing as far as forces going through Kozluk and then the transmissions over these radio statements?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: The war in Croatia was already in full swing, and since we were in a transit area, as it were, we kept watching these columns of army and non-army personnel, and we heard the war cries. And there's a multiethnic population there, and we addressed several appeals to the public, calling upon people not to listen to this war-mongering, not to heed these stories, that neighbours should take care of each other, that we should go on living in concord, that all of this would pass. We sent flyers out, and we had rallies that were attended by Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks, everybody. We socialised in different places. We simply tried to have a proper order in our own houses, as it were, so that this would not come to us as well. We printed these flyers and we distributed them in Serb, Roma, Bosniak houses. We were calling for peace and mutual respect among neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could now please have 65 ter number 1085, which is also, Mr. Banjanovic, in that binder, that blue-coloured binder that's in front of you; and you will see the number 1085.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that to appear on the screen: Were you a member of a party at that time, March/April 1992?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was always a member of the Social Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, I was president of the Local Commune of Kozluk. I had exceptionally good cooperation with Tabanci, Malesic, Skocic, and other neighbouring local communes that were inhabited by Serb citizens, ethnic Serbs. In our flyers, we expressed our views against the conflict, against clashes. It is true that we wrote this proclamation and that we printed it in several thousand copies, and that we were having it distributed. And we wanted this rally to be held in the center of Kozluk at 6.00, and everyone came --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now the flyer that you're referring to, is that 65 ter number 1085, the one that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is that dated April 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you see your signature anywhere on that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do. Right over here, I signed it. However, it's illegible. But it's true, this is an original document, because in the evening we organised this rally in the center, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When was the rally held; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we held a few rallies and a few meetings, and we sent a few flyers like this. I think that we had a big rally on the 5th, Kozluk, Tabanci, Skocic and other local communes were represented, and at these rallies and meetings, we said that we should not play into the hands of those who were involved in these provocations, that we should be in touch, all of us from these local communes, that we should have contacts, meetings, rallies, that we should socialise, talk, things like that. These flyers helped us to a considerable extent, all of us, so that we don't do anything foolish.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution moves for the admission of 65 ter number 1085.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P662. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe for the Trial Chamber the role of Branko Grujic. Do you know someone by the name of Jovo Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Branko Grujic when I said that he was a citizen of the Zvornik municipality. He was a baker by trade, and he had very good sons. His son went to school with me. And when the Serbian municipality was set up, he was the president of the Serbian municipality. I didn't have much contact with him. We would meet a couple of times. Jovo Mijatovic was an engineer working in the Glinica factory, an aluminium factory. He was a deputy, also a man who I saw several times. I didn't have any great contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What about Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Marko Pavlovic is one of the commanders of the Serbian Territorial Defence in the Zvornik area. He's a man who came from Serbia, someone who -- well, that wasn't his real name, a man who was accused in Belgrade as one of the Zvornik group. I recognised him. He represented himself as commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence all the time, and he would hold exercises at Kozluk; intimidation, he would take people away, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe certain forces and individuals coming from Serbia to the Kozluk area. How far is Serbia from Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the citizens of Kozluk were always linked to Serbia, because we worked in Loznica, Sabac, and we took our farm produces to Serbia, Banja Koviljaca, et cetera, et cetera. So Kozluk and Serbia or Loznica, it's only -- these places are only separated by the Drina River. At the beginning, we never knew of things like this. For example, Subotic came and introduced himself as being the commander of those Serb forces in Kozluk, and then Vojin Pazin came, later on -- Zoran Pazin, actually. Then the third commander turned up, his name was Marko Pavlovic. All three men were unknown to us, Subotic, Pazin and Marko Pavlovic, especially. Anyway, these three men during a short space of time where there represented themselves as the commanders of the territorial Serb municipality, which included all the armed Serbs deployed and distributed along the local communes and these various settlements.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of the takeover of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to add this: In Kozluk, the towns people of Kozluk, Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks, Roma as well, had an opportunity of getting to know a man called Zuco, who said he led Arkan's men, and a certain man called Pejic, who said he was at the head of those Arkan forces. And then we also met the commanders of the Pivarski unit or of the units Pivarski, Niski. The commander, Dragan, would rush through Kozluk with his soldiers. So in Kozluk, we had an opportunity of meeting various commanders, six or seven of them, all heads of these paramilitaries; Arkan's men, Red Berets, Zuco's men and so on and so forth, the Serbian Territorial Defence. Now, I don't know exactly, but I think it was in the month of April that all these forces took control of Zvornik. Well, the Serbs say they liberated Zvornik, but we say they took control and captured Zvornik. They were from Nis, Kragujevac, Loznica, from all those places. Arkan's men, they took control of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "Zvornik," do you mean the town or the municipality?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: They took control of the entire municipality. They only entered town. And as far as Kozluk is concerned, we were loyal and handed over all our weapons. We were not able to leave or go anywhere. We would have meetings attended by Mr. Grujic and Dragan Spasojevic and Marko Pavlovic, Mr. Pejic. They would come to these meetings. We also had meetings where religious leaders attended, Mr. Kacevenda, the Orthodox priest, for instance. Muhamed Efendi Lugovic, the Islamic religious leader, so that we in Kozluk lived that kind of life, having surrendered our weapons and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could now please have 65 ter number 1142, please. And that, too, is in hard copy, with the number "1142." Yes. And if we could please zoom in on the -- in the B/C/S version, the heading, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Does your signature appear on that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first commander of the Territorial Defence, Subotic, who came to Kozluk. After some time, Pazin, Zoran, turned up, and he had bodyguards with him and said that he was now commander of the Territorial Defence there. And the first order he gave us was to hand over all our weapons, hunting weapons, pistols and everything else, and that all the citizens should hand in their weapons, so that on the 16th of April, we set up a commission. I was the head of that commission - it was a four-man commission - who collected all the weapons and handed them over to this man, Zoran Pazin, who was the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence, and we were given receipts to say that we had handed in the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just for the record, your signature appears on page 4 in that B/C/S version you're looking at; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution moves for the admission of 65 ter number 1142.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving this document an exhibit number, a small question, Witness. When I look at this document, 87 citizens in Kozluk receive arms and ammunition, and to be more precise, it even mentions the quantity of ammunition. How many Muslims were there in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but may I just be allowed to say, Your Honour, that this is a list of citizens, us citizens, those of us who handed in our weapons to the Command of the Serbian Territorial Defence; and he said that the previous commander had been replaced, that he was now the commander, and he brought in a whole truckload of soldiers and ordered us to hand in all our weapons: pistols, rifles and so on. And we did that straight away. I set up a five-man commission and asked the people to hand over all the weapons they had. And you can see here that even the Serbs handed in their weapons. 81, Polic, Nikola, for example, and the number 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to know is this: In your commune, how many inhabitants were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 3.000, three and a half thousand inhabitants in Kozluk itself. But these were just the hunters, and it was the hunters that handed over their weapons. Well, they were the only ones who had weapons, sports weapons, and they handed them over, and nobody else had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These 3.000, there were more than 80 people who had weapons. These were hunters. What did you hunt, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pheasants, foxes. There's a lot of wildlife over there. For example, we had boars, wild boars. So we had hunting rifles, buckshot rifles, the long-barrelled rifles; but it was all registered in the police station in Zvornik. All the hunting weapons had regular permits and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 33 on the list, Nisad Semisovic hunted foxes with a Zastava, a 7,62-millimetre rifle; is that right? So he hunts a fox with a pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nijaz Memisevic, he's a passionate hunter who has the buckshot type of rifle and the carbine as well. And I said that in the Kozluk area, the hunting grounds around Zvornik, you have wild boars, and you need carbines to hunt for them. Them people had licenses to carry pistols. But, anyway, all this was regularly handed in, and you can find records of all the weapons at the police station in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 21, this person, he also hunts a fox with a 7,65 rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These persons had pistols, they had rifles, but they had the permits, licences to carry them. And they were issued those by the police stations in Zvornik, and when they handed over their weapons, they handed over their permits, ammunition and everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So everybody handed over their weapons and their ammunition. Let's give it an exhibit number now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The permits, the licenses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be Exhibit number P663. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After the surrender of all these weapons that you just described, did the situation in Kozluk intensify further?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we responded to the call from the Serbian commander, Mr. Pazin, and handed in all our weapons and permits and ammunition. We did that regularly, and there was -- it was all registered -- all the weapons were registered, and there were lists at the police station. Anyway, we were in an encirclement without food, without medicines. We were not able to leave. And now, after this handing in of weapons, there was not a single pistol in the village. So we had several meetings with Mr. Grujic and with those military officers as well to ask if people could leave. Some people needed treatment, if other people could go out and fetch food, because you couldn't leave Kozluk because of the barricade and the soldiers surrounding Kozluk. It was a very difficult situation. Food couldn't be brought in to Kozluk, or medicines, and we weren't able to leave. So I asked that this situation be resolved. We were loyal citizens, did everything lawfully, handed in our weapons on time, when we were asked to do so, so we weren't to blame for anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you have these meetings to discuss the possibility of getting food and other necessities?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we held about two meetings in the firefighters' station, the fire brigade, and the other meeting was out in the streets. Everybody rallies 'round. There was Mr. Vasilije Kacevenda, the effendi, the Muslim effendi. Then there was Mr. Brano Grujic, Dragan Spasojevic. Everyone was there, because we wanted them to see that the situation was a very difficult one, that we were closed in, no food or medicines coming in, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you go to Zvornik to have any meetings regarding these issues?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to go anywhere, because I was part of the citizenry. I was there, and I was a bit angry, because every time I asked a question, I saw that they couldn't make any decisions at all, in actual fact. I went to see Mr. Grujic, and I said, "Well, take me to the boss." And he did do that, in fact. And after the meeting, where there were a lot of people, we went to Alhos, which is a factory in Karakaj. And according to them, that's where the number-one man was. In the compound, I saw quite a lot of young people I didn't know who were well armed, their hair neatly cut. And we went into a room where there was a short, thin man. He was sitting there. We introduced each other, and he said his name was Pejic. And he said he was Arkan's main envoy and that he was the chief both of civilian and military authority there. When I talked to these people, I really did see that he was the chief person, because he would shout at Grujic. He didn't talk to him. He'd just shout out at him. He had no respect for Kacevenda or the Muslim effendi, either. So I deduce that he was the number-one man, the boss there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did he go back to Kozluk with you to see the situation for himself?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he received me nicely, and I told him that we had handed in all the weapons, that there were quite a number of people who were ill, that we were under siege and weren't allowed to leave Kozluk. And he said that that was impossible, and I said, "Well go and see for yourself."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did he do that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said, "Who's going to guarantee my safety and security?" And I said, "Well, no one. I'll go with you." And when we left Karakaj, there were about ten soldiers who left with him, and at the entrance to Kozluk they stood behind -- stayed behind. And I and this man, Pejic, the commander, and Brano Grujic, went in among the people, and he stopped at a barricade and swore at the soldiers there; why they weren't neater and why they had cocked their weapons at the people. And he even hit someone at the barricade. So I really did see that he was, indeed, the boss. And when we went in among the people, quite a lot of people were ill there, they were sickly. They hadn't received their medicines. So he turned to Grujic and said, "Grujic, you're the mayor here, you're the boss of all these people here, you're the number-one man. I want to see medicines come in straight away, food, doctors, the medical corps. I want to see all that coming in." I thought he was joking. Well, he turned around and left. We stayed on, and the next day, at 8.00, a whole full truckload of food arrives, medicines and the medical corps and doctors turn up, and they behaved to us differently. They didn't dare intimidate us and shoot up into the air. And the APCs arrived and parked in the center, and this was a kind of protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Pejic, the man you just described, was he later replaced by someone else?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a meeting with this man Pejic three times, once -- rather, twice in Karakaj and one in Kozluk, and he said he was Arkan's envoy, that he was the number-one man there. Then after him, this man Zuco turned up. That's how they called him, Zuco. He would come to Kozluk quite often with a jeep with a machine-gun built into it or onto it. He wore a military uniform. He went from one area of the battle front to another. His clothes were -- he was unkempt. He was always escorted by men wearing gloves. He was quite different from Pejic. Anyway, he came there and he arrived very often with Marko Pavlovic; and Marko Pavlovic said he was the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence. That's how he introduced himself. And the other said that he was the commander above everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when Pejic was replaced by this person you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in May, although Pejic stopped by in Kozluk once again. He was in a car. He asked around for me, and then he asked me what the situation was like. I said it was difficult. I think that was in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn your attention to the first part of June 1992. Could you describe the situation in Kozluk in that time period?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that about ten commanders arrived in Kozluk, and they all had their units. So let me repeat this once again here. Pazina -- Pazin, Marko Pavlovic of the Serbian Territorial Defence, right up until the Arkan's men, Pejic and Zuco. Then there was Pivarski and Niski, and then there were those Yellow Wasps and some other yellow whatever, and then this Captain Dragan who came with his soldiers wearing red berets, and they went all over Kozluk intimidating people and instilling fear into them. In June, since the front was quite near Kozluk, it was the Teocak-Sapna-Kalesija area, that general area, we would hear the reverberation of the explosions and fighting, and they had to go through Kozluk. It was a transit route. And we would see these units and soldiers moving -- on the move all the time, and we saw that the situation was, in fact, deteriorating and that on the battle fronts the units would go there -- or go and leave. They would come into Kozluk to loot. They would take food. They took young girls away to work in the kitchens, such as Sepac. And the situation became highly complex, and I had the feeling that everybody was running amok, that nobody held the situation under control at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. To understand properly, you mentioned "combat zone." Could you tell us who the fighters were, who was fighting whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kozluk is on the banks of the Drina River, and in and around Kozluk is where the Serbian Territorial Defence was stationed, and the paramilitaries units too, and Mr. Pejic was in command of them, that is to say Zuco, and the commanders that I mentioned earlier on. They would pass through Kozluk on their way deeper into the territory. They were moving toward Teocak, Sapna, Tuzla, and that's where the fighting took place, where those battles were fought. We just saw them passing through, the people, the units, the weapons passing through. And we noticed that when they came back from the front, there were a large number of APCs and soldiers. We didn't see any of the fights, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Your answer is a very long one, but you didn't answer my question. What I wanted to know is who was fighting against who. I understood that on the one hand there was the Serb Territorial Defence and the paramilitary units. Fine. But who were they were fighting against, these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the other hand, on the other side, there was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they were fighting against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. All right. Now things are clearer. Ms. Biersay, please proceed. We have five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before we move to the next topic, I just wanted to clarify something you said earlier. You described the first commander of the Territorial Defence as Subotic. Do you know the first name of this Subotic that you talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it changed all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Hague Tribunal took a statement from Zoran Subotic, and I demand that it be produced here and now. I haven't been provided it with the material I received for Mr. Banjanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have Zoran Subotic's statement, and if you do, why was it not disclosed to Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am, one, not sure that we do. I'll check. With respect to whether he -- it was disclosed to Mr. Seselj or not, I don't know that. I'll have to check. That we would disclose it in connection to this witness's testimony, I'm afraid I don't understand why it's relevant to this witness, based on what Mr. Seselj is saying, but we'll certainly look into it and get back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor disclosed this statement to me several years ago, so the statement was taken, that's for sure. Now, Mr. Banjanovic's statement is the only statement which mentions the name of Zoran Subotic, and I think this is a good opportunity for the Prosecutor to disclose it once again, all the material to the Trial Chamber and to me that have to do with Mr. Banjanovic's testimony, because if we look and see what it says there, we see that Zoran Subotic was mobilised as a JNA recruit, and that's what he says there, and that he was commander of the Territorial Defence of Zvornik for about one week to ten days. Mr. Banjanovic knows that better than me, but we'll be able to see all that from Zoran Subotic's statement. And he was of course a member of the Serbian Radical Party and a deputy in the Serbian Assembly; and Mr. Banjanovic is aware of that, too. But if we look at Mr. Subotic's statement, then we'll see all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it might be desirable, Ms. Biersay, to have Subotic's statement, because our witness today is telling us that Subotic was, for a time, commander of the Territorial Defence, and, as such, this can only be relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know why, Mr. President? Subotic was the commander of the Territorial Defence before the fall of Kula Grad, so before the 26th of April, and the events that Mr. Banjanovic is testifying about -- or, rather, he's going to start testifying about them, take place from the 26th of June onwards. So it's a two-month difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Can I get some clarification from the Trial Chamber? With respect to the statement, is the Trial Chamber requesting a copy of the statement? As Mr. Seselj has indicated, he already has had the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I shall ask my colleagues whether they want it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, as things stand, does not feel it needs to have this statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to transition to a new topic. I'm not sure if the Court would prefer to break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the best would be to have the break now. We shall have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Ms. Biersay, you've used up 40 minutes already.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now direct your attention to June 26th of 1992. On that day, were you summoned to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who summoned you to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: A citizen summoned me, a citizen of Kozluk, who said that I should report straight away to the police station in Kozluk, where some people from the municipality were waiting for me. It was about 40 minutes past 7.00 or 8.00, I went to the police station straight away, reported there, and I saw Brano Grujic sitting at the police station. He was the president of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik. And Jovo Mijatovic, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you met these two, Grujic and Pavlovic -- Mijatovic, excuse me, what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I went towards the police station, I saw a lot of buses and trucks. I didn't know what this was all about. When I entered the police station, we exchanged greetings, and Brano Grujic told me that I should call people to come in front of the cultural centre straight away, that we would sign something there, and that we would leave Kozluk immediately. And I said, "Why?" And he said, "Don't ask me too many questions. That's the decision, and it has to be carried out." I tried yet again to establish some kind of contact, to talk, because we had already handed over our weapons. We did not take part in any fighting or anything. Quite simply, he said to me that they had no control there any longer, that some units were threatening to come and kill us. Then I asked to give us some time at least so that we could get some of our belongings. He said that we needed to step on it, that we couldn't take anything along, that we should just go to the cultural centre, where we would sign things, get together there and board buses and trucks, and then they would send us off. Jovo Mijatovic said to me that the situation was rather serious and that they could no longer have any control over these paramilitary units, and they were afraid that one day they might enter Kozluk, torch it, and kill all of us. I went to our people in the center of Kozluk, and I said that they should slowly get ready. However, as I was leaving the police station, I already saw about ten buses, a few trucks. I saw a large number of military vehicles, army, police. I felt that these were our last moments and that we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. I wasn't sure about exactly who was supposed to be reporting to the cultural centre and be taken away. Can you clarify that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this point in time, who was left in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bosniaks were in Kozluk, part of the Roma, and a very small number of local Serbs. They told me that it was only the Muslims who had to pack up, come to that yard, and that they would be driven away in buses and trucks. They didn't tell me where, and I didn't dare ask any other questions because there were so many armed people, and I was quite frightened. Already, the situation had become exceptionally difficult. That is to say that when I returned, I said to all of these people -- and I said that all of us Muslims were supposed to show up in front of the cultural centre within the hour and that we shouldn't take anything along, that those were orders, and that we would leave from there. I came there with my mother and my family, I came to this cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did people from Kozluk who had to leave, did they go into town unescorted or were they escorted?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described seeing armed individuals in and around Kozluk; is that correct? Yes?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you went back to relay this ultimatum that had been given to the Bosniaks, how did they gather and how did they get from where they were to the centre?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a loudspeaker at that Staff there, and I asked a young man to go around telling people that we should gather within the hour and that we would be taken away, and that no one should take anything along. There were armed people in different uniforms standing in front of all the houses, and in the center of Kozluk there were a few military vehicles, transporters and tanks. There were large forces of the Serb Territorial Defence, paramilitaries as well, Zuco's Wasps, Arkan's men, and all the others. They were there in Kozluk. Upon arrival in front of the Culture Hall, a man was fired upon. His name was Galib Hadzic. Part of the houses had already been torched. We didn't even get to leave town. What was the most difficult for me was that our mothers and sisters were searched by these very same men, in a very abrasive manner, humiliating, as if they were carrying money in their bosoms. And we found that very hard to take. They were really taking it out on us. As we were signing there, they filled up the buses and trucks with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I can just slow you down just a little bit. You mentioned Galib Hadzic. You said that he was shot at. Was he wounded?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was seriously wounded in the leg, and we bandaged it and carried him onto the truck. He lives here now with his family, in Vienna, but he has serious consequences due to that shooting. He was shot at only because he was a Muslim. They brought pressure to bear against our mothers, our sisters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are giving us a detail that makes me think of something. We can really understand and picture the scene you've drawn for us, but there is a detail that has called my attention and should call everyone's attention. You said that there were tanks. If there are tanks, it means that there is presence of the army of the JNA, or does it mean that the paramilitary units had tanks as well as the Serbian Territorial Defence? So I'd like to know whether the tanks mean that the JNA was there or whether they mean something else. Could you shed some light on this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until that morning, only military armoured vehicles, APCs were passing through Kozluk, tanks from the theatre of war, but they didn't spend much time in Kozluk. That morning, there were military APCs and jeeps there and tanks, and the Serb Territorial Defence was there too. The army was there in uniform, the police, paramilitary units, a large concentration of military and paramilitary units that day in Kozluk, because their task was to expel and deport about 2.000 of us Bosniaks. I really don't know what belonged to who, but I know all the units were there; the military, the paramilitary, the police, quite a few of these men who had already started torching houses. They already shot this man who was peacefully walking along in the column, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that about 2.000 Bosniaks were being deported. This means that it was a large-scale operation, but can we infer from this that the operation was controlled by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know under whose control it was, but we were loyal. We had handed in our weapons. We were peaceful. We were promised help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, that's not the question. I don't want to know whether you had been loyal or not. All I know is that you were on the scene, you were there. So better than anyone, you are in a position to tell us whether you believe that this operation was controlled. And given the resources that had been deployed there, I'd like to know whether you believe that the JNA was in control of all this or not. You're the only one that can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that on that day, I was in Kozluk, and it is correct that the army was there, and army units, and APCs, and the police, and armed forces, and everybody. I'm sure that there was coordination, as far as this operation was concerned. After all, it involved 2.000 men. Tanks were there, and the army, and there must have been coordination and control. Why would they otherwise be in Kozluk? They were at the very center of Kozluk. Guns were pointed at Bosniak houses in the center, and next to every house there were military and paramilitary men. So it is for sure that I claim that there was this coordination between the military and the paramilitaries. And Mr. Grujic told me that he had just been instructed to tell me that, but I don't know who it was from up above that ordered him to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I just follow up on the Presiding Judge's question, because you told us just a while ago that Mr. Grujic had told you that all the Muslims had to leave Kozluk and that they had to do so because -- I think you said that no one no longer was in control of the paramilitaries. This does not coincide well with the fact that the JNA was there also, and presumably better armed. So are you implying that Mr. Grujic was trying to put the blame on the volunteers or what is the correct understanding of what you have testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quote what Grujic said to me. The situation is complex, that they could no longer have control over these paramilitary units, and quite simply that someone could enter Kozluk and kill us. And I said, "Well, the police is there, everybody is there. Why would they kill us?" I mean, we handed over our weapons. And then Mr. Mijatovic, an MP, walked up to me and said, "Mr. Banjanovic, the situation is a difficult one. We are just conveying this to you as a decision and an order. It is no longer under our control." I just know that these units kept passing through Kozluk and that at first, in June, the situation was extremely difficult, that they even launched a few attacks against Kozluk itself, these territorial Serbian units, and they were shooting over and above Kozluk. I really had no idea what was going on. Believe me, I was just one of the citizens there. But that morning, soldiers were there, tanks were there. Then these different men of Arkan's were there, the Serb Territorial Defence, the Serb police. They were all in Kozluk, and they all had this one task; to expel us from Kozluk in a very hard, harsh, brutal way, without taking any of our belongings with us; insulting our mothers and sisters, searching them, wanting to whether they had any jewellery; boarding us onto buses and trucks as if we were sardines. People were being shot at, houses were being torched. The situation was complex and highly difficult for us Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were the Bosniaks who went towards the cultural centre, were they only from Kozluk or were there Bosniaks from other parts?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: All Bosniaks who happened to be in Kozluk on that morning were supposed to report in front of the cultural centre, to sign there, to be seen there and board the buses. That was an order. We had to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there any Bosniaks from Skocici [sic], and I apologise for the pronunciation?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you say the name of that town? How do you say it correctly?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Skocic. It is inhabited by Serbs and Roma and Bosniaks, and these Bosniaks came to Kozluk and they had to leave with us. Those were the orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter number 1464; and I will also, after that, ask for 1463.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So in your binder, you'll have the number 1464 as well. So if you keep on going. There you go. Do you recognise 65 ter number 1464?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what is that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a list of persons who had come in front of the cultural centre, who signed statements to the effect that they were voluntarily leaving everything behind to the Serb authorities. And a statement was read out to us as well. That was the list of persons who had set out, households, family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
