utterances.text: We'll get to that document that was read out to you. But for now, focusing on this document, do you see your signature on the last page of that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is this document dated 26 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The stamp on page 1, whose -- do you recall what authority stamped that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the stamp of the Serb municipality of Zvornik, and they put the seal and stamp of the Serb Territorial Defence. And, well, what was read out to us was this letter that they brought in. They opened it, they read it, the letter of this commander of this Serb Territorial Defence. And this list was made, and this is the list of men who boarded the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The document that you're looking at, 1464, that is a list of the people who were leaving what village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the cultural centre in the center of Kozluk, they all gathered there, signed. They searched us, and then they put us onto buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Looking at the first page, the title, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what does it say?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says that this is the list of persons who are leaving Kozluk in an organised manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on this list, do you have the heads of households in one column and then the number of the -- number of family members in the other?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. For example, Vehid Marhosevic, he was the head of the household with nine family members in two houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution would move for the admission of 65 ter number 1464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P664. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could now look very quickly at 65 ter number 1463.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that a similar document that was produced on June 26th, 1992, as well?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The people on that list, from what village did they come?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: The village is called Skocic. It's a neighbouring village to Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And does it also have a similar stamp on the first page?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the Serbian municipality and Serbian Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On page 2, did you sign this document on June 26th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, we'd move for the admission of 65 ter number 1463.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it shall be given Exhibit number P665. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could now, Mr. Registrar, now be shown 65 ter number 4222, which would be towards the back of the Court binder, 4222.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you describe that something was read out to you. Directing your attention to the document before you, 65 ter number 4222, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber how it was read out to you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: When they had packed all the people up into the vehicles, the trucks and trailer-trucks, the representatives of the Serbian Territorial Defence opened an envelope, and this was what was written inside, and there was the stamp of the Command of the Serbian Territorial Defence, saying that they were sort of sending us outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On that document, there's some handwriting. Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had one document, and then I specified how many households from Skocic, how many from Kozluk, a total of households' members and so on; and I said that was in 17 buses, three trucks with trailers and so on. And then I recorded here the number of the Red Cross of Loznica and Dr. Zoran Nikolic's number, who helped us a great deal at the time when we crossed over into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the second sentence from the top. Could you read that out, if you're able to, in the copy that you have?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says these persons who have expressed a desire to avoid mobilisation have been allowed to move out. That's a terrible lie. Nobody mobilised us, nor were there any Muslim units. There are only kind of mobilisation. This is just a lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just so the transcript is clear about where your reading stopped, could you read the last word in that sentence so we know where to end the quote?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: "... allowed to move out."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, was that true?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked us anything. We were ordered to come in front of the dom. We were all searched. We were mistreated, sworn at, shot at, loaded up into trailers and trucks. They didn't discuss anything with us or talk to us. This envelope was handed to me and opened up, and they just said, "You're going there, and see what's going to happen there." There was no question of any mobilisation into Muslim formations or anything like that. That's a sheer lie. Who would have been in Zvornik there to mobilise us? And nobody asked us anything. Even this statement that we were leaving there property of our own free will behind, nobody asked us any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution would ask for the admission of 65 ter number 4222.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before asking Mr. Registrar to give us a number, I would like to have a technical detail. I'm looking at the signature of Major Marko Pavlovic, and I see that in the English, it says, "For the commander of the VTK, expansion unknown." According to you, do you have any idea what this "VTK" stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the document that I received wasn't signed by Marko Pavlovic. Somebody signed for him and put "for."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had noted this, and I wanted you to tell me about this, because in the English it says, "For the commander," whereas in the B/C/S the "for" is in front of "Major." So it looks like there's a commander of the VTK, then there's a Major Pavlovic, and somebody who signed on behalf of Pavlovic. You're right. But do you have any idea what this "VTK" stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All we knew was the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence, Marko Pavlovic. We didn't know any of the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you want an explanation, I can give it to you, but only if you wish to hear it. When the JNA withdrew on the 19th of May, what remained was the local reservists mobilised into the JNA, and instead of the then Territorial Defence, which was subordinated to the JNA, the military territorial command was set up, VTK, which was the intermezzo between the JNA and the Zvornik Brigade of Republika Srpska which was established sometime at the end of June. I'm not quite sure what the date was. So this is "vojno teritorijalni komandant," military territorial command, and speaks of the unity of the army and the Territorials, and it's the interim period between the JNA and the Zvornik Brigade of Republika Srpska, army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you agree with this explanation given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I hear of it. I don't know. All it meant to us was the Serbian Territorial Defence, led by Marko Pavlovic. And these people changed, from Subotic to other people, and this Marko Pavlovic was the last person who expelled us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have an explanation on the transcript, and we can always refer to it. Let's have a number for this document, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P666. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did all the Bosniaks from Kozluk leave in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, we all rallied together. We got in and left. Then later on we learned that some 12 or 13 people stayed behind and that they were killed; Bosniaks who did not want to leave with us. They were killed by the soldiers in those units that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described the buses and the trucks with the Bosniaks on them. Were there other vehicles that went with the ones containing the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the head of the column, there was the Serb police vehicle, and at the end of the column, another Serbian police vehicle, so two police cars escorting the column to Sepac bridge and across the bridge over into Serbia. And we parked there along the banks of the Drina River and waited to see what was going to happen next.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you taken? By "you," I mean the convoy of all the buses and the trucks carrying the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: They opened this letter, read it out, and said we were going to continue our journey on into Serbia. And we continued towards Sepac bridge and the crossing into Serbia. Kozluk was full of soldiers, vehicles. Several houses were set afire. It was very difficult. It was difficult to leave your town and your home just because you belonged to another ethnicity. And when we arrived -- when we arrived in Serbia on the banks of the Drina River by Sepac bridge, lots of paramilitaries collected their people, wear black gloves and different uniforms, and they went from the trucks to the buses, searching for young girls and women to take them off the vehicles. And I told the people that they shouldn't get out of the buses and trucks, and that the doors should be kept closed, that people should stand up against the doors and prevent them from being opened. And I knew Mr. Dragan Nikolic. He was a doctor in Zvornik, he lived in Zvornik, and he was the head of the Red Cross. And I asked the -- or, rather, he lived in Loznica. And I asked the Loznica police to come in, and we were very frightened, that that half hour was a long half hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So where was your first stop? Was it in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: In Loznica, by the Drina River, the embankment there, just when we had crossed the bridge. Loznicka Polje is what the area is called. And then they wanted to pull out the young girls and women from the buses and trucks, and they shouted out all kinds of things to us. But when the Loznica policemen turned up, they turned up with four or five police cars and sent them packing, and then they encircled the area with police cars, and then I went to the police station in a police car. And they we sent a letter from the Red Cross to Belgrade. And while we waited to get an answer, they gave us fruit juices to drink and sandwiches to eat. And there were quite a lot of children and sick people, and they didn't give us any -- hadn't given us any food up until then, or we didn't have money to buy anything. So the situation was really very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: From the time that you requested the assistance of the Red Cross until the time that you had a response, how much time elapsed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: The police came straight away, half an hour later, and sent these people packing, the ones who were attacking us and who were beating us and swearing at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My question was unclear. You described that you asked the International Red Cross for help; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What kind of help were you looking for?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we asked them to tell us where we were being taken so that we would know, and we asked to be given some water and food. And the people from Loznica helped us. They sent us food straight away, and some fruit juices for the children and so on. And the letter was sent to Belgrade, and several hours later a confirmation arrived stating that we could go further on towards Subotica. We were given permission to move around Serbia or something like that. But the police was with us all the time, and so nobody abused us anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could now have 65 ter number 1465, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, what you are saying is a little bit confused. I shall try to sum up what you have just said. You crossed the bridge, and you find yourself in Loznica. There, there are soldiers and paramilitary units. They are excited, they want women, and you decide, in those trucks, in those buses, not to move, and the women are not to get off the buses. Then the police arrive very quickly, from what I understand. The police come from Loznica. The police protect you and drives these paramilitaries away. Now, from that time onwards, you will be getting aid, since you told us that you got something to drink and something to eat. And it seems, according to what you said, that a courier is then sent to Belgrade, and this is to let you know where you are to go from there. After a short while, a document arrives, and this document specifies that you need to go to Subotica. Is that how things happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how it was, and this -- they put me in this one police car, drove me to the Red Cross, and that was all as you've just stated. And when the letter arrived, they said we would be transported by train, that we'd go to Ruma, and then from Ruma, that we would be transported by train. That was the telegram, the dispatch that was sent back to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you were present - I wasn't, but you were - did you have the feeling that the local authorities, amongst others the police, were in full control of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The policemen you spoke to, did they know that you had arrived or did they discover it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I say with full responsibility that this was all a staged setting, a scenario, and that they knew where we were going, where we were. And I saw that by -- on the basis of their conduct. But then they just sort of took me to this Red Cross, and we waited there just to make a show of it; but I'm quite convinced that it was all a scenario, that everybody had their role, and that that group of bandits who was there was not there by chance, those who mistreated us. And it wasn't by chance that the police turned up in two or three police cars. If you ask me, it was all well managed and staged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as you are concerned, all this was staged. But what was the purpose of it, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Well, quite simply that in that part of Republika Srpska, the Bosniaks should be expelled, because we did represent a problem in that Drina belt. You know, 2.000 Bosniaks in the Drina belt along the transit road, that posed a problem. We were an obstacle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that from top to bottom and bottom to top, everyone agreed to drive you out, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- seemingly among the 2.000 people that were there, no one was killed, no one was beaten, no one was ill treated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the process of expulsion itself, Galib Hadzic was wounded with a bullet, and the greatest insult was that our sisters and mothers were searched, and they touched them on their breasts and elsewhere. That was the greatest insult. And then this group of hooligans attacked us in Loznica, and allow me, Your Honour, to tell me the torture that we were exposed to. We were beaten up in Ruma when we set off from Loznica in and trucks. Allegedly a train was waiting for us in Ruma, but it was a cargo train for cattle, used to carry cattle, and more than 50 people launched stones at us and hit us with chairs. Many people were injured, women and children. It was a terrible journey; no food, no water, beaten up and mistreated, and very well escorted by the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned what happened in Ruma, but perhaps Ms. Biersay was about to mention this. You've anticipated that. I give you the floor back, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could now look at 65 ter number 1465, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether or not you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was in Loznica that they showed me this material. They said that the government in Belgrade had given permission for us to travel through Serbia and that we were moving towards Subotica. And the police told us that we would go to Ruma in those trucks, and then in Ruma, that we would board trains -- a train going to Subotica, and then we'd see further on towards Hungary and Austria. We just wanted to get as far away as possible, because in Loznica the paramilitaries began gathering, and the policemen, so it was a difficult situation there, too. But, yes, I do recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: The 26th of June, the same day we were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you stay in Loznica for the night?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not -- no, no. We all went to Ruma together.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in this -- you've described what you believed to be the purpose of this document to the Trial Chamber. Did you personally have a copy of this document? Did you keep one with you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't really know. I was just happy at the time, when I heard that Belgrade had decided that we could travel further and that there would be a train waiting for us in Ruma. I don't remember. But I know that they wouldn't let us go before this arrived. Now, what happened next, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Several hours, two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you next go to Ruma, Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in buses and trucks, we reached Ruma, which is a town in Serbia, and we were told that we would be getting into a train and that we would go further on on our journey by train.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did the 1.822 of you get onto this train?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was difficult to board the train. It wasn't a proper train, it was the trains that are used to transport cattle, so a group of people -- and a group of people arrived, and they threw stones at us and beat us, and said that we were Alija's army and called us Turks. And ten people were wounded while boarding the train. We were beaten with some pieces of wood, and I was injured myself. And then the police turned up and sort of threatened them. Well, I must say, to be quite frank, that when the police arrived, they didn't beat us anymore. But up until then, they threw stones at us and threw chairs at us; and they broke two or three small windows or slits on the train, all the windows were broken. But otherwise, we were all packed into the cattle cars. And then we went on towards Subotica. We had no food. Quite a lot of people were ill by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before we move to Subotica, at this time we would move for the admission of 65 ter number 1465, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can we have an exhibit number, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P667. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Biersay, can I just ask if this letter was the letter they received in response to the witness's call from the Red Cross office to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you respond to the Court's question?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived at the Red Cross office, apart from the food and assistance, they said that they had to send a letter to Belgrade, to ask permission from Belgrade whether we could pass through. And I said, "Well, send it to whoever you like." And then they brought in the food and all the rest, and an hour or two letter they said that a letter had arrived from Belgrade, giving us permission to carry on on our journey. So that's what I knew. I didn't have an insight, I didn't actually see all that, but that's what I was officially told; that the commissariat or the government or the authority in charge of the refugees could be given permission and that there be a train waiting for us at Ruma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: On the train, in your group, were there any pregnant women?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Merima Husic was present. There were quite a lot of sick people as well. Ten or twelve persons had been injured by the stones thrown at their heads or backs. We were badly beaten up then. They were saying that we were Alija's soldiers, Turks, whatever. When the police came to Ruma, then they shooed them off, and then nobody hit us anymore. And then we continued on to Subotica, and then we stopped at Subotica, at some sidetrack. A baby was there by then. Merima Husic had a son. He's here in Vienna now. There were quite a few sick people. We didn't have food, we didn't have anything. It was a very difficult journey. Beaten-up people were travelling in cattle cars. It was just so difficult. And then, as we were there for a day and a half, then some people started bringing us food, water. Then they took care of the baby. It was really hard, it really was hard. 2.000 people in these train cars. And then the Red Cross came, quite a few people came. I asked TV people to come and to film this. Different TV stations came from home and abroad. And then there were these babies, and sick people lying in the train cars and outside. It was a horrible scene. No one deserved to be mistreated in that way, really. Then these people from Subotica came. They said that they'd take us to this place called Palic, as if it were some sort of camp or something. Then they indeed transported us to this camp. There was a barbed wire around it. There were tents there. We slept in meadows. There was a single point for water, where 50 or so people washed their faces and washed up. It wasn't a classical collection centre; it was a camp. The thing that offended us the most and that made us worry the most was that we recognised these same people with beards who had been walking about Zvornik and Kozluk, who stole things from us, killed us, who stood on the bridge at Sepac, Loznica, Zvornik. We were simply so afraid... they kept this camp at Palic --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One minute. If we could now look at 65 ter number 4201, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just see this map here, and I see Subotica marked on the map, and I see Palic as well. They called it a transit centre, but it looked more like a concentration camp to me, because there was barbed wire, tents, no facilities whatsoever; just a field toilet. The people who are supposed to take care of people there scared them more than anything else. We were transferred to this place called Palic, and some good people came there from the Suboticanka factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: How long did you personally spend in Palic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: About ten days or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time where people were able to obtain passports?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we arrived in Palic, then they selected the people who had passports, and then they took them as if they were preparing visas for them, if people had money, although in our case we didn't have any money, they had searched us and we didn't have anything on ourselves; so about 200 people did not have passports.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could now have 65 ter number 4218, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How were people able to obtain passports?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, we asked some people from the Red Cross to have the top people of the factory that was in Subotica to come and see us. It was a chocolate and sweets-making factory, because they had a good relationship with the Vetinka factory in Zvornik. So they came to see us, and they brought us some fruit juice and some sweets; and then we asked them to help us obtain passports, because 200 people did not have any passports. The following day -- the following day, people from the police came. Then the management of the Suboticanka factory came, and they gave us a cheque for all of us to have our photographs paid for, passports, everything. They paid the police with that cheque, and then the Red Cross said, "You are fortunate because the Suboticanka factory gave money for you to get photographs and passports for you." And then photographers started coming in, taking pictures, and they started issuing passports.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it would be 65 ter number 4218.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know Esma Hadzic and Saha Hadzic? And that's also -- 428 is in your binder as well.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who are they?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: These are inhabitants of our Kozluk who were there together with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I just want to use this so that we can show the Trial Chamber just an example of the types of passports that people were able to obtain. So if we could go to the next page of this exhibit in B/C/S. And for the record, this is the passport cover for Esma Hadzic. If you could look at the hard copy in front of you. We'll do it the old-fashioned way. And if you could turn to page 6. At that page, the one you just passed, if you go back one. There's a stamp on that page that you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What authority issued that passport?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Secretariat of the Interior in Subotica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is that passport consistent, the one for Esma Hadzic, the type of passports that were issued to people while they were in Palic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. All the people who didn't have a passport got this passport. Photographers came, took their pictures. They handed over the pictures, and then we got this kind of passport. Who didn't have this kind of passport couldn't go any further. That is to say that we all got this kind of passport.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, we'd move for the admission of 65 ter number 4218, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when I look at this woman's passport whose name has mentioned, Hadzic, Esma, I realise that on page 17 of her passport, there is the stamp of the Republic of Austria, dated the 17th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The witness may need assistance, Your Honour. The e-court doesn't seem to be working, so if the usher could help the witness locate the proper page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, leaf through the passport and turn to page 17 of the passport. It's not very difficult to do. All the passport pages are numbered. On page 17, I don't read German, unfortunately, but I have the feeling that this is a visa to enter the Republic of Austria, which seemingly entitles the holder of the passport to remain there until the 17th of March, unless I'm mistaken. Witness, if a passport has been issued, this means that the Republic of Austria knew that there were a lot of people who were in transit and who were going to enter Austria. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to say here that a number of people from this transit centre, or Palic, were picked up by relatives. They would come from Austria and take them. Some went to Austria, some went to Germany, others -- well, what mattered was that these 200 people got passports and that then we would leave in different groups, as they organised things for us in Palic. The Austrian and the German authorities had to have this kind of information; that Austria was supposed to be entered by 500 people or 1.000 people. I assume there was this kind of communication. I do not have such documents, I do not have evidence of this, but if 2.000 people are sitting and waiting to be transferred to some other country, somebody must have known; either the police, or the border services, or whoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then, I mean, you had some responsibilities in your municipality, and you're a deputy right now, so did that not imply at the time that there had been agreement between the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Austria, or an agreement between the Red Cross and the Republic of Austria? What do you think happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have any document, but there certainly is an agreement among these commissioners for refugees, because it's not 10 people, it's 2.000 people here, and then visas had to be obtained, papers, documents. So my personal view is there must have been coordination among commissioners for refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What about in your case; did you obtain a passport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also got a passport, and I was in the last group of some 100 persons who were put up in Hungary, Najetad [phoen], this transit centre. There must have been coordination, if some of us were sent to Najetad, some others to Austria, yet others to Germany. We were just pleased to get passports and to move on, quite simply to flee from this environment. The situation was so bad in Palic, from the point of view of health, sanitation, and everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume there must have been a stamp on your passport, Hungarian stamp, according to which you were allowed to enter into Hungary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, all of us, I mean, this group who had passports, took care of our transport and visas and everything. I mean, everybody had this type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, just to have a sense of time: To issue 2.000 new passports and have them included -- and have visas included in them must have taken quite some time, so how long a time did it take from the moment you arrived to Palic and until you had your new passport issued ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I said that 80 per cent of us had passports and that about 200 were not there, and this factory took care of those people, about 200 of them. And they brought ten photographs or whatever there, and they took care of all of this within a day or two. And as a group would get passports, then they would take them away. I personally did not keep any records. I don't have any evidence of this. People would leave tents. They would be told, "You've got a passport. You can leave now." The camp was being emptied, and we were glad to see that. So it was a bit less than 200 passports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Biersay, the Registrar just told me that you just have a few minutes left, so please try to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were these passports, the ones that were issued in Palic, were they free?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were paid by the Suboticanka factory. They paid for the pictures and the passports.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How were passports issued? Were they issued individual by individual, or were they issued to groups -- were they issued per family?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were group passports, there were individual passports. At any rate, it was the MUP in Subotica that took care of this and this organisation. Believe me, I did not keep abreast of that. I was there, just like others.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor's question is not appropriate, whether families were being issued passports. Group passports were never being issued, except for children who were minors. Parents could only have their young children in their own passports, and there were no other group passports. Perhaps the witness did not understand what the Prosecutor's intention was, and that's why he gave the kind of response he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have rectified this, anyway. Witness, tell us whether these passports were individual. Even if, in a family, there were minor children, the name and age of the minor children are on the passport of either the mother or the father; that's the way it was, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time, we'd move for the admission of 65 ter number 4218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P668. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that would conclude the Prosecution's direct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Ms. Biersay. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor, and we'll have the break later on, in about 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Banjanovic, I don't have many objections, in view of your testimony. According to my information, you enjoy a very high reputation among the Serbs and Muslims of Zvornik, and this is attested to by the current office you hold. I'm just going to dwell on some details now. In your statements, you mention Seselj's men at one single point or, rather, one single man of Seselj's, Zoran Subotic, who was commander of the Territorial Defence in Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had the opportunity of seeing this Mr. Subotic only once. I don't know how long he was there, two or three days. To tell you the truth, I really don't know exactly what it was I said in my statement, whether I said he was an MP of the Radical Party or whatever; but I know that once I did meet him, this was only during the course of a few days, and Pazin came immediately, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For the witness's convenience, I have prepared a binder with his statements, so if Mr. -- if we could please give this to the witness, and if Mr. Seselj could just identify which statement he is discussing, because there are several. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's nothing that is to be contested here. I'm not going to deal with the witness's statements anymore. It is 2001 and 2002. That's what it says here. I find that a bit strange, two days in two different years. It must be some kind of a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is this statement from 2001 or 2002; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember. But as I have already said, he just introduced himself as an MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that he was commander of the Territorial Defence from the 5th until the 13th of April, 1992 only; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. It was just for a few days. He appeared in Kozluk only once, and then I realised that he was there only for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did he behave towards you? What kind of a man was he; was he fair, was he proper?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very fair and proper. I just met him once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since the OTP took this statement from Zoran Subotic in 2003 and 2004, in paragraph 42 of this statement he says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we do not have the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- that he received call-up papers from the JNA and that he was mobilised in Mali Zvornik, and that he was deployed in a tank unit of the Tuzla Corps that was commanded by Captain Dragan Obrenovic. Do you find this convincing, what he says here? Have you heard of this tank unit of Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know Captain Obrenovic. I know that he was the lead of this unit, these tanks, and that they were located in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Nowhere else do you mention Seselj's men, because you personally did not have any contact. This is a colloquial term for the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the territory of Kozluk, I did not come across any, or in the places where I was, and I said clearly that they were Arkan's men, Zuco's Wasps, the Serb Territorial Defence. I did not have occasion to come across members of Seselj's units or commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Banjanovic, you could not come across them because on the 26th of April, they all left Zvornik. Do you know that on the 26th of April, Kula Grad fell?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You had this collective attempt, all of you inhabitants of Kozluk, to move in the direction of Tuzla. You mentioned that, but you did not mention the date. Do you think that you could recall the date?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could not recall the date. There were several attempts, because Kozluk was considered to be a place where everyone found refuge, and really there weren't any killings, there wasn't any unrest, as opposed to other villages. At one point, there were a lot of people gathered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A lot of Muslims from the surrounding villages who had fled?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And all of it thanks to your reputation, because you were a man who did not advocate the war option; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: To this day, I'm against wars, and I will always be against war because it hurts everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What -- your village is one of the few Muslim villages that did not arm itself at all; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I'm just going to say one thing, that Kozluk is not 100 per cent Muslim. There are a number of Serbs and Croats and Ruma living there, and we were not aware of any option of arming. We had quite a few hunting weapons and pistols. Well, we did have that. The head of every household had that, say, when there was a patron saint's day or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, it is a majority Muslim village, right, and there were some Serbs and only a few Croat families?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 90 per cent are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, you said several times that you tried to move out, so you had left en masse; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not that we had left or set out, but we were lined up there in the centre and we were bothered by these barricades around there and also the fact that these units were passing there. Quite simply, the situation was such that we were confined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was this April or May?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was April and May, and everything culminated in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On one occasion, personally, the Serbian bishop from Tuzla came, Vasilije Kacevenda, and the Muslim mufti, Muhamed --

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Lugovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, and they together tried to persuade you not to move out; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: They said that we should not move out, that everything would be fine. And then we had this meeting with this chief man over there, because they could not offer us any guarantees. We said, "Who is the guarantor," and they said, "In Karakaj," this page. And then with Mr. Kacevenda with the assistance of Muhamed Efendi Lugovic, we came to see this chief man that I spoke of a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As an experienced and smart man, you realised it was in the interests of the Serb authorities that you Muslims remain in Kozluk, that it was in their political interest, because you did not take part in the war conflicts and this newly-established Serbian authorities were supposed to express goodwill and to show this as an example of life together; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it was an obvious Serb interest, however something then went wrong; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What went wrong was after the 19th of May, when the JNA had to withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Had you heard of this ultimatum of the Western powers that the JNA withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You haven't heard of it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. And you said several times that the situation became chaotic in Zvornik, that people did not know who was controlling who; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I said the situation had become exceptionally difficult in Kozluk, and as a citizen of Kozluk, I went to Zvornik only three times because we were in a total state of isolation because of the barricades; and no one could leave Kozluk. It is only three times that, with this special pass, I managed to get to Zvornik, and twice to this Staff of the Territorial Defence in Zvornik with this special permit. So this isolation and these barricades, whatever, and the fact that there was a shortage of food and medicine, it was quite simply very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you did hear that at the end of May and beginning of June, different paramilitary groups were killing Muslims in some parts of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You had to hear about that; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that was already a considerable number of Muslims who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I knew was that there was a conflict between the paramilitary units and that quite a few Bosniaks were killed by way of retaliation for what happened in the battlefield. So towards the end of June, there was -- there were these disturbances in Zvornik, clashes among the paramilitaries: Zuco, Marko, and those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you hear on some occasions they arrested Brano Grujic, Marko Pavlovic, and they even took them out for some kind of an execution, and then they let them go?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot talk about that, because I do not have any knowledge of my own. I know that they mistreated everyone and that a number of Muslims were, indeed, killed. And now the bones of these persons are being found and exhumations are taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In a few locations?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in town, and this has been happening over the past ten days or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness and Mr. Seselj, please observe pauses between questions and answers. You're moving too fast, and the interpreters cannot follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree that the killings occurred at the end of May and beginning of June, that that's when most of the killings of Muslims occurred, civilians and prisoners? Can we pinpoint it to the end of May and beginning the June?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that in my town of Kozluk, that a man was killed at the beginning of June in a meadow just because he was a Bosniak, and I know that in Zvornik the situation deteriorated and there were quite a few killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that when you left Kozluk or soon afterwards, a special unit of the Republika Srpska, a police unit, arrived in Zvornik, disarmed the paramilitaries and their leaders were arrested and taken to the prison in Bijeljina? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. On the road to deportation, I didn't know that, but later on, several years later, I did receive that information; and it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say who the leaders of those paramilitary units were, the main ones. There was Pejic. He was Arkan's deputy, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: He said he was Arkan's number-one man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you see that Brano Grujic had to stand to attention in front of him on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: When Effendi Lugovic and Kacevenda and I went there, he didn't allow Brano Grujic and Dragan Spasojevic to enter; but they had to stand outside and stand to attention, and so I really did see and realise that he was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he slapped Jovo Mijatovic on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Now, you mentioned Zuco, Pivarski and Niski, and those are the names that keep cropping up here all the time. Now, you also mentioned Captain Dragan; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He appeared in the Zvornik area, to the best of my knowledge, when the JNA left, that is to say, at the end of May and beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: My information tells me that Captain Dragan, in the area of Divic, that he was then stationed or put up at the motel called Vidikovac, and on one occasion lots of young men were running around wearing red berets, and people said that they were his men. So those were my encounters with those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were his soldiers who had red berets on their heads; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that from Mikica and some other paramilitary commanders, and I asked them who they were, and they said they were Dragan's units. Anyway, they had red berets on their heads, those young men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that they had some strange insignia, a cross, and then the four -- something that appeared to be four "S" letters back to front?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't notice that, and I didn't like to look at them, because they were running around and I didn't know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you know that he set up a training -- some sort of training centre in Divic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that the army of Republika Srpska expelled him from Zvornik soon afterwards because members of his unit went around Divic looting?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that, neither about the looting nor the fact that they had been expelled. I was in total isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was just testing whether you knew that, and the Prosecution has documents about when Captain Dragan was expelled from Divic. But as you say, you know nothing. Then let's move on. Tell me now, please, when you testified in Belgrade, because I had been provided with all the transcripts, towards the end of your testimony there, they confronted you with Brano Grujic; right? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I testified in Belgrade for eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. And Brano Grujic claimed that for five days before you left Kozluk, you were in Zvornik, and that you had a meeting there with him and with Pejic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true. I never had a meeting with Grujic and Pejic, except in Kozluk, when we were there all together among the 10.000 other people. So that was our joint meeting, but never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If you denied that, I'll move on. Now we come to the 26th of June, and Brano Grujic and Jovo Mijatovic arrive. They come to see you, and they say that they have no control over the events in had Zvornik, and that great danger loomed from some paramilitary gangs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: They said, and I quote, "Mr. Banjanovic, in one hour's time all the Muslims around the dom have to leave, and that's an order." And I asked why, and they said that it was an order, that they didn't have any more control, and that the clashes were taking place in Zvornik and that we run the risk of being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they seem upset and flustered?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any stability in them. Mijatovic came up and he said, "Bratska [phoen]," that's what they call me, "the situation is serious. You have to leave." And I saw, by his appearance, that that's what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in is this: It's a long time ago and it's difficult to remember all the details, but according to you, did they seem to be truly concerned about your fate or were they people who were just play-acting to make you leave?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think they were concerned about us at all. They were just forced to come and say that. Quite simply, they were more afraid for their own lives and their own skin. The clashes had broken out. Well, I don't think they were in control of the situation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So I understand it, that the person who was in control of the situation forced them to come and tell you that.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. I think that you've been frank and sincere in answering my questions; and I think that that is quite true, that they had absolutely no control over the situation, that it had escaped their control, that the paramilitary gangs and bands were running amok and controlling the situation.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you made a list of these people who were leaving Kozluk and then a list of people leaving Skocic, and you said that you had to sign a statement saying that you were leaving your property to Republika Srpska. However, we can't see that on the basis of these documents. Was that a separate statement?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: This statement -- this list was signed, so the list was compiled and copied in several copies. And then when they searched us, we signed it and said that we relinquished our property. I never saw the list with the signatures, but it's true that we did sign them, and we were very -- we were searched in a vulgar manner, especially the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what I don't quite understand here is that on the list, it says here that they were persons who were moving out of Kozluk in an organised manner. There's no trace of anybody leaving their property to anybody. So that's a little strange, whereas you're a serious man; and it's quite clear to you that even if you signed over your property under such conditions, that it would not have the force of law?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everything was clear to me at the time, Mr. Seselj. The situation was very difficult. People were armed to the teeth. There were four or five military units. Commanders, some were drunk. People began shooting. All around, the situation was extremely difficult, and we thought that we would be killed. We didn't know that we were going towards Loznica until we actually got into the transportation and until that envelope was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Loznica, you were given police protection there, and you were taken to the Red Cross of Loznica; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: We parked across from the bridge, and then we were attacked by some people who were drunk and were looking for women. And then a police car turned up. I went up to them. Well, we didn't leave until three or four other vehicles had arrived, and then I was driven to the Red Cross with a police escort, and I was received there very nicely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was the Red Cross of Loznica; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Loznica Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it wasn't an international Red Cross of any kind, as the Prosecutor said in chief?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: The man's name there was Dr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to the information I've been provided, you had no contacts with the International Red Cross at all until you left Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, nowhere, nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And all the assistance you were given, modest but which came at a good time, was given to you by the local Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Loznica Red Cross and the Subotica Red Cross, those two organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said here that it seemed to you that all this had been stage-managed. First of all, you were attacked by an unruly band, and then the police came to provide protection. Now, do you have a detail that you can tell us about -- to confirm that it was really the police who was behind these gangs and bandits and whatever?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't claim that for sure, but when you have 50, 60, 100 people hurling stones at you, a lot of people were injured. I was injured, too. I was hit by that, too. And then a patrol of two or three men arrive, and everything calms down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about Ruma.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We haven't got to Ruma yet. I'm asking you about Loznica now. Just as you crossed the bridge, you stopped, and you were in Serbia; right? And there was a group of people there who provoked you, attacked you, tried to seize the women and girls, and so on; that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that group armed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when the police arrived, the police managed to calm the group down?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: They called up reinforcements, and four more police cars turned up. And they formed a convoy and encircled the people and made them leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have any tangible proof to show that the group had come to attack you, having been incited to do so by the police, and then that all this was stage-managed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you can't actually then say that the police was behind all this, can you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: In my statement, I said that this coordination did exist between the Secretariat or -- the Red Cross, the Secretariat and the police, and this transport to Ruma, and then the train from Ruma to Subotica. That's what I meant when I talked about cooperation. There was some system, some link in the chain. Now, as to the police and the paramilitaries, I'm sure the police did their job. Why would they look for our mothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you know that this is an area where there was a war, and you could -- if you were bearing weapons, you would just be fined. It was only later on that there was a ban on carrying weapons, later on. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, this coordination that existed between the Red Cross and the police, well, we can't say, actually, can we, that the crowd, the unruly crowd that attacked you, could be thought to be part of that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, part of Loznica is -- and the inhabitants of Loznica, part of Subotica and Ruma, because we were beaten up on the territory of Serbia, that's where we were mistreated. We were provided an escort. We had this train in Ruma. It's all mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, you know that in every town, we have what is known in German as the "Lumpenproletariat," that is to say, an unruly crowd ready to loot at the earliest opportunity; and you know, for example, in the centre of Belgrade I was attacked by an unruly crowd, and I had to take out a pistol and shoot up into the air to stop them. But if you show them that you can stand up to them, then they tend to flee. And here you have the police standing up to them, and they fled. That's what happens; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you were given some food and fruit juices for the children, and you set off for Ruma. Did you have a police escort from Loznica to Ruma?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they just escorted us through the town of Loznica. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they didn't escort you further?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So anybody who wanted to leave the bus, for example, could do so and to go their own way; to relatives in Serbia or whatever, if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: How could we leave? We had nothing. We were told that a train was waiting for us and that we would be put up in the train and then go to these Western countries. So for any normal person, that was the best way out, because we knew what the situation was like in Serbia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. There was an economic crisis, a blockade set up by the Western powers, and life was very difficult, there was a lot of poverty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So now you arrive in Ruma and you board this train; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were promised the train, and we were told that the train would take us to Subotica. And when we arrived, all we saw was the locomotive and the freight trains, freight cars. So we boarded up there, and we were at the train station, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During your testimony in the Milosevic trial, footage was shown of that train, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll continue on with Ruma in a minute, but I believe it is time for the break. The tape is almost over. We will now break for 20 minutes and resume at five after 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, let's take a look at this document that you were shown by the Prosecutor and has already been admitted into evidence once again, and I'm referring to document -- or, rather, the document which arrived while you were still in Loznica from Belgrade, from the Commissariat or commission for refugees. Let me just find it. The document 1465. May we have it put up on the e-court, please? I'll have to take a moment to look for it because they put it together in the wrong order. While you were in Loznica, and as far as I was able to understand, it went on for a few hours, you were waiting for a reply from Belgrade, from the Commission for Refugees, a decision pursuant to your request; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then that decision did arrive, and it says there: "We considered the written statements of 1.822 persons in 17 buses, three trucks and trailers and two passenger vehicles from Kozluk, Zvornik municipality," and they said that without any pressure and of their own free will, they wished to leave the territory of Yugoslavia and go to the countries of Western Europe. Now, I'd like to know where these statements were sent from, saying that you wanted to travel to Western Europe of your own free will, et cetera. Did you send that out from Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the Red Cross of Loznica. I went there and asked assistance for these people, and then they said we had to send a letter to the Commission for -- well, anyway, to the commission. They sent it several hours later and said that they had received a reply, and that we could pass through Serbia, and that they would line up this train from Ruma to across the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you sign that in the statements in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They just wrote it down, typed it out on a typewriter. Perhaps the list that I had -- perhaps they photocopied that and sent it. But we didn't sign anything in Loznica, nor --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, did it say on the list that you were going of your own free will and without pressure? Did somebody add that to the list, then?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say, but I assume that -- well, on the list that already existed, it said that we were going voluntarily, because the list was used when the Territorial Defence in Kozluk wrote those letters and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they refer to the fact that it was your right to choose where you wished to live, that's what it says in this document, where you wish to reside?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Banjanovic, that throughout the war, in Serbia, 70.000 Muslims were officially registered from Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were refugees in Serbia and stayed there, some forever and some for as long as the war was on?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that a part of the Bosniak Muslims were in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, when Srebrenica fell, did you hear that a part of the Muslim soldiers swam across the Drina River into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that event, because I don't know it myself. I did hear that some people swam across, that they were captured there and returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean that you heard they were returned to Republika Srpska, not a single one was sent back? Let me tell you this: When Zepa fell, more than 900 Muslim soldiers, almost a whole brigade, crossed the Drina River and were accepted in Serbia and they were put up in the collections centre on Mount Tara, accommodation centre, where the International Red Cross came straight away, and none of them were brought back to Republika Srpska, all of them were enabled to go abroad. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I won't insist upon that. When you don't know just say you don't, and I'll move on. I won't insist and belabour the point. Now, when you arrived in Ruma, without a police escort, as far as I understood it; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think they escorted us out of Loznica and pointed us in the right direction, and the train was waiting for us at the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that means that the police didn't expect an incident to happen over there. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When the incident took place, you were already in the train; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we were getting off the trucks and trailers and buses, we would get into those freight cars where -- which were used for cattle, and then at a distance of 50 metres they would throw stones at us and say that we were Alija's soldiers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many people were there who did this?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe 50. They were young people, mostly, youngsters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, the mob was organised in a spontaneous fashion?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were organised or not, but I know that we really were beaten up pretty bad. Stones were thrown at us. And then we carried our sick and wounded. There were quite a few elderly people who were beaten up. I don't know for what reason. The police showed up there, too, and then when the police arrived there, then the stoning stopped. On the train that we took, all the windows were broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that already by then, there were about 200.000 refugees in Serbia, most of them from Croatia, but some from Bosnia-Herzegovina too?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that in Serbia, there was a great deal of bitterness because of the fate of the convoy of JNA soldiers that was leaving Tuzla, and between 150 and 200 of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I lived in total isolation. I already told you that for four or five months, Kozluk was in total isolation, and I went to Zvornik only about three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The police intervened and then drove the mob away; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then you arrived in Subotica. You spent a day on the sidetrack, and then you were taken to Palic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How were you taken to Palic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is no railroad to Palic, as far as I know Subotica.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any details. I just know that we got to Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Probably on buses?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably, and it was very hard for us because we were about a day and a half or two on this sidetrack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there were tents put up in Palic; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was barbed wire, gates, then water outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you think the barbed wire was there so you would not run away or was it for the sake of your own safety, so that someone wouldn't attack you again?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when the barbed wire was put up there, but I'm sure that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was summertime, so one could be under a tent?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We were out there in the fields and the meadows. The situation was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No one was hungry; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was food, and we had to wash up outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, no one was expecting you outside, waiting for you outside?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was food there and tents and improvised water facilities, and there were people there that we recognised who were in -- on the bridge at Kozluk, Zvornik, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you not secured by the police there in Palic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was no police in uniform?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any. There were some uniformed men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were military uniforms, different kinds of uniforms. It looked more like paramilitaries than policemen from Loznica and Ruma and places like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you know, but I am in prison here with a few Serb police generals, and they guarantee that it's only people in blue uniforms that were around you and that it was impossible for anyone else to be there around you. Is that possible that you may have made a mistake, in terms of what you remember, in terms of your memory?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that we were put up at this camp with barbed wire in Palic, and the most difficult part of it was that we recognised these men, these warriors who were at the Zvornik bridge, et cetera. There are several people who signed statements to that effect, and we know the names of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know, it seems impossible to me that you saw these people in Zvornik and then you saw them on the other side of the Drina River, and then you saw them in Subotica. After all, it's about 200 kilometres away, right, or perhaps even more than that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, at Sepacki bridge, what happened happened. A group of armed men, scavengers, they were asking for ours girls. 2.000 people saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I believe you, Mr. Banjanovic, I believe that, and I'm sure it was terrible out there. But what I find unbelievable is that these people showed up in Subotica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't talking about those people, Mr. Seselj. I talked about three or four men that the citizens recognised as having been in Zvornik. I didn't say that it was at Sepacki bridge. In Subotica and Palic, my fellow citizens recognised some people who were in Kozluk and at the bridge, and they know the names of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know agree with me that this is rather unreliable, this recognition?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible that a mistake was made, but we organised our own safety, by way of prevention, by not sleeping at the same time, all of us, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, regardless of whether you were asleep or not, you were not armed, so if someone attacked you, you could not be saved in any way?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's my assumption. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if somebody wanted to attack or rape my sister or mother, I would have slit their throat with my teeth. That would have been a weapon enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But there was good police safety and security there, at least in my view. We have yet another document here that was shown by the Prosecution, and that was 4222. Could we see it again?
