This is a document that was signed by someone on behalf of Major Marko Pavlovic, and this request is being sent to the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to allow safe conduct for the persons on this list, persons going to Hungary. And you will see that they were going there of their own request, not under duress, and they said that they wanted to avoid mobilisation into Muslim formations. I find this to be ridiculous, too, because you could not have been mobilized into the Muslim formations, right, and had you had wanted to do that, you would have done that before the war started or when the war started, but not when all of Zvornik was practically in Serbian hands. I find this ridiculous, too.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we would have established detachment, divisions. We would have been armed and we would have fought. We were against war, Mr. Seselj, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, both speakers are speaking at the same time, which is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was taken away from you were hunting guns and pistols for which you had permits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please slow down. The interpreters are complaining about the fact that you're both speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It doesn't say here that you left your property to Republika Srpska. It says here that families that opted to move out are aware of the risk to the property that they are leaving in the zone of war operations, and their attention was drawn to the fact that the authorities in Zvornik cannot fully take over responsibility for the property they're leaving behind at their homes and apartments. So it doesn't say anywhere that you signed off your property and that you said that you were leaving it to someone else. They simply said that they could not guarantee the safety of that property and they could not be responsible for its fate. That's what is written here.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: These two documents are different. The document that you're reading out was in an envelope. When we all sat down, then they opened it and they gave it to me. Up until then, I didn't know where we were going, and no one else knew, either. And the other one is the list that people signed. I never received that list, and that list simply wasn't there. Every citizen signed, in front of the cultural centre, a document stating they were leaving their property voluntarily, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think that this is strange. The OTP from The Hague got all the documentation of the Zvornik municipality from the war period, even the payrolls and everything else, and quite simply there is no document where you are voluntarily giving up on your own property. Even the OTP from The Hague could not find that. That's why I wanted to draw your attention to that. Perhaps that did exist, but it's not there now. Now, look at this one piece of information that I find interesting. You said that almost all of you had passports, 200 of you didn't have any, and then new passports were obtained for them; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And on this piece of paper, it says that out of -- out of 1.822 of you, only some of you had passports. So only 169 had passports, in accordance with this document; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't remember now all this math and sums of mine, but I know that we just got this assistance from the Suboticanka factory in Subotica, because they had good relations with the Vetinka factory in Kozluk. They visited us, and then I asked for this. And then the next day, they brought a cheque. And the police came and they said, "Now get these people passports." How many passports, I really don't know, because at that time, I was not a controller of any kind. I was just an ordinary citizen, like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, I don't hold anything against you. Who could remember exact figures after all those years? I don't find that to be strange at all, and I don't think it is strange at all that you do not recall how you were transferred from that train car on the sidetrack from Subotica to Lake Palic. That's not strange at all. This is simply blocked in one's memory, and it is very hard for a person to remember every little thing. I fully understand you, but the only thing I have are these documents. I was not in Palic, and on this piece of paper it says that only 169 people had passports. All the rest had to be issued with new passports. Now, you say it was the factory of Suboticanka that paid for this. However, you should remember that these taxes for issuing new passports were not very high. Right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any money, and then they wanted to give us a truck of fruit juice, and we said, "No, we don't really need that." They gave a cheque for us, but I don't know how much it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me just tell you one thing, Mr. Banjanovic. I know that for humanitarian reasons, this tax is not levied at all and that people didn't have to pay for it; I mean, refugees in Serbia at the time. Quite simply, they were issued with passports, free of charge, and I really would have been surprised if someone had made you pay in your situation. And we both remember that at the time, the tax for a new passport was a symbolical amount; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how big it was, but I know the people from Subotica gave this cheque to the policeman in front of us, and they said, "This is a gift to the citizens of Kozluk from us." I really don't know whether it was one Deutsche mark or a thousand, but they were really fair. They brought the cheque, and photographers came on the same day and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the food of good quality?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was communal eating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, 1.800 people were there. Communal eating, there is no other way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we ate it. I mean we didn't ask for hotel accommodation. There was food, there was water, and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No one was hungry?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. Let us look at this document now, 4218. That is the passport of Esma Hadzic that we've already seen. Do you agree that this is a normal SFRY passport, a passport of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, just a regular passport? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an elderly woman, and it's certain that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Look at the first page of the passport. There is a white piece of paper stating "Esma Hadzic"?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is this the cover page of the kind of passport that we all had in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Serbia did not issue any different passports in 1992, although the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, this was the only passport that both you and I had at the time; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know who was issuing what. I just know that this was the Yugoslav passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But there was no other passport. We see basic details here pertaining to Esma Hadzic; that she was born in Bijeljina, that she lived in Kozluk. And on the next page, we see her photograph. On the previous page, we see her identification number. And now we see that her two children, Fadil and Avdo, are also registered or, rather, her husband and son?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now we see their photographs, too. Let's look at the next page. Is there anything unusual here about this passport? A husband and wife who have children who are minors can get a collective passport; right? So what we see here now -- rather, let's look at page 11. It says that the passport was issued by the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. They were authorised to issue passports. Like in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina that issued passports; right? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, the Secretariat in Subotica, the passport was issued on the 29th of June, 1992. You left Kozluk on the 26th of June. You spent several hours in Loznica. You arrived in Ruma. You travelled to Subotica, and then you arrived in Subotica on the 27th; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 28th, you were transferred to Lake Palic; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It could not be any different. The periods involved are minimal. Esma Hadzic received a passport already on the 29th. You see what it says on this passport? The passport is valid from the 29th of June, 1992, until the 6th of June, 1997; so she got this passport for five years, valid for five years. So within those five years, she could freely travel abroad and return to Serbia any number of times without any restriction. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: However, here it says that a tax of 550 dinars was levied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, you are right. So the factory did pay?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of it was paid for. The people took a lot of trouble to help us. The factory really gave money for the photographs to be taken and to have the passports issued to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're right, and I didn't even notice this myself. Do you see that the passport was valid for five years?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So during those five years, Esma Hadzic, her husband and son, could enter Serbia without any restrictions an unlimited number of times and could leave again, if they so wanted; right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We see further on that they could turn to the consulates of the Republic of Yugoslavia, and if they happened to be abroad, they could have their passports extended there. As a matter of fact, they were treated here like any citizen of Serbia; right? Am I not right, at least as far as the passport is concerned?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we know full well, Mr. Seselj, how we were treated; surrounded by barbed wire, in a tent, sick, unable to walk around very much, transferred in groups, and no one had any idea when we would go. Say a mother and son would be transferred to Germany and then others to Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just two brief questions. In Subotica, did they have a better place to put you up?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I know Subotica quite well, but I cannot remember where else you'd have better accommodation for this big group of people. Palic is a tourist resort. There are some bungalows out there, as far as I can remember. Palic is the most beautiful part of Subotica, isn't that right, on the lake?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with Subotica or Palic. They put us up on this meadow that was surrounded with barbed wire, in tents; and we were beaten up, and how, in Loznica and in Ruma. Wasn't that nice? And babies were delivered along the way. Beaten up, without food. I tell you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The very fact that you left your home shows how difficult your journey was.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: We did not leave our homes. We were expelled. We did not leave Kozluk of our own free will. We were expelled on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We agreed that it was paramilitary gangs that expelled you, and they dominated over the political authorities there. And you confirmed that to me.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Brano Grujic, president of the Serbian municipality, sent us to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, again the speakers were speaking at the same time, and we could not hear what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm just following what you said, Mr. Banjanovic, and I have no reason to quarrel with you. In my view, you are a fair and frank witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that you can follow, but we can't, because the interpreters can't keep up the pace; the court reporter can't either. So you need to wait for the witness to finish, and the witness needs to finish until you have finished. Otherwise, we have to stop there, because we really can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, I have another paragraph here. Saha Hadzic. Go a little further on. Or, rather, another passport. Her particulars are there. I'm leafing the pages, and I come to page 11, and it says here that the passport was issued on the 29th of June, 1992, and that it's valid until the 6th of June, 1997; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the dates are the same. The Prosecution could have shown us some more passports. I wouldn't have been able to see them, had I not been provided them by the Prosecution. But, anyway, can we draw the conclusion from this that all the passports were issued regularly, in regular fashion, standard procedure, et cetera; do you agree? You had to provide a personal document of some kind, where the personal ID number was visible, and then photographs were taken on the spot, and you needed more than 1.600 photographs. And they took your fingerprints, too. You don't remember that, do you, but I remembered. So they took everybody's fingerprints, and then all the documents were sent to Belgrade to be checked out in the register for citizens of the SFRY. Do you know that all SFRY citizens were recorded into a register?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that we paid 550 -- we paid a lot for this, 550 at Mrs. Saha's.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the factory paid for you with a cheque. You didn't pay, but you were given a passport, and it was valid for five years. And you received the passport under regular procedure. That's what I wanted to tell you. It was normal, regular procedure; isn't that right, Mr. Banjanovic? Now, you said that you were in the last group to leave Palic; right? In the statement here, you said that you were there for eight days, and now you say you were there for about ten days?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember how many days exactly. They were terrible days, as far as I was concerned, days of horror, and I know that as the groups were given passports, they went off. We didn't know where they went. Some went towards Hungary, some went to Austria, Germany, as we later learned, so that those families were broken up. A mother would go one way, the others another. It was difficult to control the situation because there were such a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But do you agree that, for the most part, it wasn't done according to the will of the state organs of Serbia, because first of all you had to receive permission from the Austrian and Hungarian authorities to take you in?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So do you realise that the Hungarians, for instance, didn't want to have 1.800 people descend upon them all at once, but that they would like to take them in two groups?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as we went towards Austria and Germany and so on, there must have been some coordination, but what it was, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they groups of 200 people?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So roughly 200, groups of 200. So that had to be organised, too. You couldn't do that straight away. Now, Mr. Banjanovic, you spent some time in Austria?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Najetad all the time, Hungary, and then I went to Austria. I, wife, mother and so on, children, some were in Austria. Then I returned to Najetad, and then I went to Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when did you return to Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 2000, I returned to Kozluk. And in 2001, my family came to Kozluk; my wife, two children, my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the other people, when did they return to Kozluk, your fellow citizens?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: We had an organised return in 2000; the first group, 18 of us, and then there were more, because there were Serbs from 28 municipalities, 4.850; so we couldn't all go back at the same time. We decided to do this in stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So your houses were preserved, and Serb refugees were accommodated in them?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 4.850 Serbs from 28 municipalities were living in Kozluk at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then the authorities of Republika Srpska relocated them gradually, found other accommodation for them, and you returned to your own homes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then the authorities of Republika Srpska started to invest larger sums of money to reconstruct the infrastructure in Kozluk, to build the waterworks, networks, which network and so on?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the government of Serbia and the respective ministries provided resources for drinking water, for a clinic, for roads. And Kozluk is part of Republika Srpska, so that we asked for the resources, financial funds, to be provided, because there were Serbs living there, not only Muslims, but Serbs and Croats, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you and your fellow Muslims who had returned to Kozluk were satisfied with the conduct of Republika Srpska towards you after your return; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the government of Republika Srpska and the respective ministries and their support to us in our return, we are satisfied; and we have prepared a number of projects to open a number of factories. But we consider that to be quite normal, because we're part of Republika Srpska, part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's our government and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have a piece of internet information here. While I had my legal advisers, they were able to provide me with that. And on the 27th of April, 2007, in Kozluk, you welcomed Milorad Dodik in song. Well, that might be a little exaggerated. You might not have been singing. But you said that you were satisfied with the government's treatment of you and the amount of assistance you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Arkan's commander, Mr. Pejic, was greeted in Kozluk, and when he saw that the people were ill, when they returned weapons, we received medicines. As far as Dodik is concerned, he fulfils all our requests, so we have every respect for him and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where people who returned to Republika Srpska; we respect the laws, the constitution of Republika Srpska, and consider it's our job to fight for getting drinking water, roads, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, you didn't complain about Pejic, Arkan's deputy, who was the be all and end all over there. Your main trouble started when he left Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, our main troubles were actually the war. The war caused all the trouble. It caused Pejic and Pavlovic and all the other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, what's interesting for me here is the following: Do you know where Rastosnica is?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Rastosnica is one of the largest Serbian settlements in Sapna municipality, and Sapna is located in an entity called the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Sapna was part of Zvornik municipality at one time; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And according to the Dayton Accords, the municipality was divided and Sapna appears now to be a newly-formed municipality over there; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Sapna is a new municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right, new municipality. And it's the largest Serbian village which is to be found within the Sapna municipality?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1992, that village was attacked by the Muslim paramilitaries and that a lot of the inhabitants were killed and all their houses burnt; did you know about that, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, I don't know that, because I was totally isolated. But later on, I did hear that there were war events going on there. How, what, against whom, I don't know. I was in total isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I happen to have a piece of information from 2007 to compare the situation in Kozluk, and you say you're satisfied by your treatment of the -- by the government of Republika Srpska. And I see here that in Rastosnica, in that same year, only 180 of the burnt 1.050 Serb houses have been rebuilt and reconstructed, whereas in Skakavci, which is close by, only 20 out of a total of 350 Serb houses have been reconstructed. They haven't reconstructed their school, or clinic, or anything. And from that I draw the conclusion that at least in the area where you reside, in that border belt, Muslims are much better treated, Muslim returnees in the Republika Srpska, than Serb returnees in the Muslim-Croatian federation, their treatment there. Do you agree with me? Perhaps this isn't -- you don't like hearing this politically, it doesn't suit you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your information, Mr. Seselj, is not correct. In Rastosnica, we have the most modern school, and the clinic is the most modern and has been reconstructed. But Rastosnica is a large settlement where there are a lot of little areas and settlements. Now, I can't be asked to assess who is better off where, whether it's better off in Sarajevo, in The Hague, or wherever. But as far as Kozluk is concerned, we carry projects to the government; and we have invested a lot of time and effort to create a better tomorrow for ourselves, because clinics are not only for Muslims. Serbs are treated there, and the road through Kozluk, Zvornik, Bijeljina, the road there, well, people use it from all over, from Pale, Banja Luka. The waterworks that Mr. Milorad Dodik invested over half a million marks in caters to four or five local communes; so all this is of general interest to all of us and to all our benefit. And what I want to say is that the government did provide us with this, but we fought for it. We went and asked them for it. That does not mean that the citizens of Rastosnica should have the same thing, but they have to be active, invest time and effort, and keep going to the authorities to demand what they want, because unless you do that, you're not going to get anything. So I want to say that discrimination in the area where I live really does not exist, and I'd like to say that very publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Banjanovic, but I wanted to use this internet information to show you that when it comes to Serb refugees, that the situation is quite different. But I won't insist upon that. I understand that you need not be exposed to any great mistreatment to put you in a difficult situation. But what I respect is that you testified publicly in the Slobodan Milosevic trial, and the trial in Belgrade, and now my trial here. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I appeared everywhere publicly, without any code names or pseudonyms or whatever, and I was -- and I always recounted the things I know firsthand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I think your testimony was almost identical, as far as any testimony can be identical. When you testified in the Slobodan Milosevic trial, for instance, and then went back to Kozluk, did you have any unpleasantness of any kind when you returned?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this testimony of mine is not of my own free will. I live in Kozluk. My child goes to school with other Serb children. I am one of the functionaries that returned to Kozluk. I don't live in Sarajevo or Tuzla. I live in Kozluk. So please believe me when I say that in -- among my own people, just like among the Serb people, there are still people who want to opt for the war-mongering variant; so I'm always afraid that my child might be seized or various -- I've received threats, and I've reported that so people who these people are who made the threats to kidnap my child and so on. But, anyway, everything I say, I say publicly, and I'm doing so here today, because what happened happened. God forbid that it should repeat itself, because war is always the last option.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, I say that you testified honestly here, sincerely here, and I hope that you won't have any unpleasantness when you go back to where you live, and that is my wish, because you testified honorably. And I'd like people to come in here to tell the truth, how they experienced it. We can, of course, disagree. We can have a different approach, but all I would like to hear is truthful testimony. And I hope that this will continue, and that when you go back, you won't have any unpleasantness. Thank you for testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Biersay, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you for having come to The Hague to testify in these proceedings. I wish you the best for your safe return home. I hope everything will be fine for you in the future. I will now ask our usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me now turn to the Prosecution and Mr. Mundis. As far as tomorrow is concerned, we have a witness scheduled. I believe he's already in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The witness who's listed for tomorrow is here in The Hague and will appear in the courtroom tomorrow at 0830. We still have no information with respect to the other witness, and I believe at this point in time it is clear that he is not going to be testifying this week. That leaves us with just the one remaining witness for this week, and I do know that my colleague Mr. Mussemeyer would like more time than the one hour allocated; and I believe Dr. Seselj also wanted more time allocated for the cross-examination of that witness. So I wouldn't anticipate we'd have any problems in [indiscernible] the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long had you planned in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honours, we had requested, if the 92 ter was denied, that we be given two hours for the next witness. So we would respectfully ask that we be given two hours and that Dr. Seselj be given two hours. I believe the Trial Chamber, in denying the 92 ter motion, had given each side one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this will be a viva voce witness. The Prosecution will have two hours, and Mr. Seselj will have two hours. That seems very reasonable and justified. Let me remind you that this witness will be testifying on the deliberate line of conduct. I believe that is what he's here for. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely agree, now that you've said "two hours." That's what I was going to ask for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Two hours for the Prosecution, two hours for the Defence, and we'll probably have some questions from the Judges. I believe that the witness will stay overnight and will be finished on Thursday. But at least we have time, so we can take advantage of this time. This being said, Mr. Mundis, I have my computer in hand -- a calculator in hand. Every time a witness comes, I subtract time from your allocation. At the end of this week, you'll have about 20 hours left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That accords with where we expect to be at the time we stop for the winter recess, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me wish you all a pleasant evening. We will meet again tomorrow at 8.30 a.m. Have a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
